stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: Why do scores differ even within one method?
stages.miniPlan: Three students, their group, and their score.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a row to highlight the same dot; distinguish individual scores from group means.
stages.reference: One dot is one student's score. A group mean is that group's average; the grand mean is the average over all students. Different students can score differently for many reasons, even when they receive the same teaching method. The drawing describes these scores; it does not establish what caused them.

stages.title: The Research Question
stages.question: Is the gap large compared with ordinary variation?
stages.miniPlan: Same mean gap with small versus large within-group spread.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust signal or noise separately with a fixed seed; keep the other quantity constant.
stages.reference: Keep the average gap fixed and change the spread inside the groups. The gap becomes easier or harder to see. We judge it against the spread and the sample sizes, rather than deciding from the gap alone. A sample is the people we measured; the population is the wider group we want to describe.

stages.title: The Rules of the Game
stages.question: Which assumptions support this comparison?
stages.miniPlan: Assumption → visual symptom → appropriate response.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch between unequal spread, outlier, and repeated-student examples; state that design cannot be diagnosed from a plot alone.
stages.reference: A residual is a student's score minus their group average. The normal-error assumption concerns these errors, not a requirement that all raw scores share one bell curve. Similar variance means similar squared spread. Equal group sizes can help with some mild departures, but they do not repair dependence. Repeated-measures or mixed models are possible approaches when the same person is measured several times.

stages.title: Variance Decomposition
stages.question: Where does total variation come from?
stages.miniPlan: One observation's distance to its group mean and the grand mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal within-group and between-group squared distances in sequence; show their sum with correct weighting.
stages.reference: For each student: score − grand mean = (group mean − grand mean) + (score − group mean). Square means multiply a gap by itself. Add the squared gaps across students to get sums of squares, or SS. With the ordinary group-mean fit, total SS = between SS + within SS. Do not interpret the between part as a proven causal effect.

stages.title: The F-Statistic
stages.question: Why divide one mean square by another?
stages.miniPlan: A two-row MS-between / MS-within comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Link each term of F to its visual component; compare a null-like and separated-groups scenario.
stages.reference: F = MS between / MS within. Under the equal-means model and the ordinary test assumptions, both mean squares estimate the same error variance. A large ratio can challenge that model. The denominator is the within-group mean square, not the total sum of squares.

stages.title: Degrees of Freedom
stages.question: Why are only some values free?
stages.miniPlan: Two editable numbers, a fixed total of 30, and computed third number.
stages.interactionPlan: Correct 8 + 15 + 7; transfer the constraint to k−1 and N−k using group counts.
stages.reference: Three values with average 10 must add to 30. If two are 8 and 15, the third must be 7. For k groups and N students, between df = k − 1; within df = N − k; total df = N − 1. The numbers used to estimate averages explain these subtractions.

stages.title: A Worked Example
stages.question: How do the numbers produce F?
stages.miniPlan: SS → df → MS → F arithmetic receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through the displayed dataset calculation; synchronize the worked values with the current preset.
stages.reference: Use the separate small example in the receipt: between SS 120 divided by df 2 gives MS 60. Within SS 270 divided by df 27 gives MS 10. Then F = 60/10 = 6. These printed numbers are a separate worked example. The interactive picture reports its own current data.

stages.title: Reading the ANOVA Table
stages.question: How do I read an ANOVA table?
stages.miniPlan: Column glossary with SS, df, MS, F, and p.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus or tap a table cell to highlight its geometric meaning; keep explanations available without hover.
stages.reference: The table keeps each source of spread beside its SS, df and MS. To judge F under the null model, use between df for the top and within df for the bottom of its reference distribution. The null model says all population means are equal. Rejecting it does not identify every differing pair.

stages.title: How Big Is The Effect?
stages.question: Does a small p-value mean a large effect?
stages.miniPlan: Same effect size under two sample sizes.
stages.interactionPlan: Link eta-squared to the variance partition; separate association, uncertainty, and causal interpretation.
stages.reference: Effect size describes how much separation there is. Eta-squared, η², is SS between / SS total. In a separate example, 3456/3852 is about 0.90: about 90% of the observed squared spread is associated with group membership. That still does not prove causation. Eta-squared, partial eta-squared and R² are not interchangeable in every design. Name the measure you report.

stages.title: Post-Hoc Testing
stages.question: Which groups differ?
stages.miniPlan: Three pairwise differences with intervals.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal adjusted pairwise comparisons together; show the multiplicity family and avoid an automatic unadjusted t-test sequence.
stages.reference: Testing many pairs creates more chances to flag a difference by chance. A planned contrast combines groups for a question chosen in advance. A follow-up procedure such as Tukey's HSD can control false alarms across all pairs under its assumptions. Say which comparisons and adjustment you used. Some pairs may remain uncertain even when the overall F test rejects equal means.

stages.title: Enter Two-Way ANOVA
stages.question: Why add a second factor?
stages.miniPlan: A 3 × 2 design grid.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a method–sleep cell and reveal its observations; preserve the distinction between factors and outcomes.
stages.reference: With three methods and two settings, there are 3 × 2 = 6 combinations, called cells. A balanced design has the same number of observations in each cell. Missing combinations can make some comparisons impossible to separate. The study design determines which effects we can estimate.

stages.title: Cells & Marginal Means
stages.question: How do we average across the other setting?
stages.miniPlan: Cell means, row means, column means, and weighting.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a selected average from its cells; flag that equal averaging here assumes the balanced teaching design.
stages.reference: In the printed example, method A averages 60 indoors and 70 outdoors. Giving both settings equal weight gives 65. If many more students are indoors, an average giving every student equal weight will differ. State what the average is meant to represent. The separate sleep example uses cells [82,74,66] and [62,66,70], with method averages 72,70,68 and overall average 70.

stages.title: The Interaction Effect
stages.question: What does an interaction mean?
stages.miniPlan: Difference of differences with a concrete numeric example.
stages.interactionPlan: Move from parallel to nonparallel lines; crossing is optional, and observed patterns alone do not establish significance.
stages.reference: Indoors, B − A is 8. Outdoors, it is 2. The difference of differences is 2 − 8 = −6. The sign tells us how the gap changes. Nonparallel sample lines show an interaction in those sample averages; a population claim still needs uncertainty and a suitable model. Small random departures from parallel lines are not proof on their own.

stages.title: Building the ANOVA Table
stages.question: How is two-way variation partitioned?
stages.miniPlan: Method / sleep / interaction / residual contribution ledger.
stages.interactionPlan: Add one component at a time; retain clear balanced-design assumptions behind the decomposition.
stages.reference: For balanced data, add the SS parts for A, B, A×B and within-cell error to recover total SS. Each effect's F compares its MS with error MS. In the separate sleep example, A beats C by 16 under high sleep, while C beats A by 8 under low sleep. Averaging the settings can hide that reversal. With unequal cell sizes, the model and sums-of-squares convention affect which question each test answers.

stages.title: Reading the Two-Way Table
stages.question: What should I read first in the output?
stages.miniPlan: Interaction, then conditional comparisons, then qualified main effects.
stages.interactionPlan: Select output rows to highlight relevant lines and cells; remove claims that crossing alone confirms a population interaction.
stages.reference: An interaction can make a single main-effect average misleading. Read the cell means and the particular differences that answer your question. State the design, weighting and model, especially when cell sizes differ. A non-significant interaction test means this test did not give enough evidence; it does not prove the interaction is exactly zero.

stages.title: Caveats & Recap
stages.question: When should I choose a different analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Design/variance condition → suitable method family.
stages.interactionPlan: Run a short scenario choice; distinguish invalid reference inference from an uncomputable F statistic.
stages.reference: Inspect raw points, group spreads and unusual scores. Check why an unusual value occurred rather than deleting it for a preferred result. Rank methods such as Kruskal–Wallis concern distributional or rank differences, not automatically the same mean comparison as ANOVA. Report group estimates, intervals, a named effect size, and any adjusted follow-up comparisons. Match repeated or clustered data with an appropriate design-aware method.

anova.title: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
anova.intro: Compare the averages of several groups. See how the gaps between groups compare with the differences inside each group.
anova.prerequisite: Averages, fractions, and reading a dot plot.

stages.title: The Prediction Problem
stages.question: Why can fitted predictions differ from reality?
stages.miniPlan: True function, noisy observation, fitted prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Use a known simulated population and label which quantities are hidden in real data.
stages.reference: For a teaching model Y=f(x)+ε, f(x) is the average outcome at input x and ε is remaining noise. A fitted model estimates f using a training sample. Real data need not separate neatly into visible signal and static. Even an excellent mean prediction cannot remove every individual outcome's variation.

stages.title: Bias: the average miss
stages.question: What does a consistently rigid model miss?
stages.miniPlan: Several underfit curves on repeated samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Resample with a fixed population and show their mean prediction as well as individual fits.
stages.reference: At a fixed x, bias is E[estimated f(x)]−f(x), with the average over repeated training samples. It can come from the model family, penalties, estimation procedure or data problems. A straight line applied to a curve is one illustration, not the definition of all bias.

stages.title: Variance: changing fits across samples
stages.question: What makes a flexible fit unstable?
stages.miniPlan: The same x with predictions from several training samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare repeated fits; separate variability across datasets from residual noise within one dataset.
stages.reference: Variance is the spread of estimated f(x) across training samples. An unstable fit can respond strongly to small sample changes. Overfitting means learning sample-specific details that harm new-data performance. A flexible model is not guaranteed to overfit, and raw outcome variance is not the same as fitted prediction variance.

stages.title: The Error Decomposition
stages.question: Where does the squared-error decomposition apply?
stages.miniPlan: Noise + squared bias + variance at a fixed input.
stages.interactionPlan: Accumulate terms from repeated simulated samples; label empirical estimates and squared-error conditions.
stages.reference: Assume new zero-mean noise is independent of the training sample. For squared loss at a fixed x, expected error = squared bias + prediction variance + noise variance. These averages concern repeated fits and a new outcome. They are not calculated by relabelling the residuals of one dataset. The lab can show them because the teaching data generator's mean is known.

stages.title: Interactive: The Trade-Off
stages.question: Must error always follow a neat U-shape?
stages.miniPlan: Actual simulated error versus a schematic tradeoff curve.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub complexity and inspect repeated-sample results; avoid treating the illustrated sweet spot as a universal law.
stages.reference: More flexibility can change both bias and variance, but neither must move in one direction for every learning method. A minimum in one noisy validation curve is not a universal sweet spot. Compare uncertainty, repeated data splits and practical usefulness alongside average errors.

stages.title: The Testing Problem
stages.question: Why is training error insufficient?
stages.miniPlan: Same model on seen versus unseen examples.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal an untouched development holdout and ask which score supports selection.
stages.reference: A low training error describes fit to the rows already used. Resampling creates held-out comparisons from limited development data. Each fit must exclude the rows used to score it, including from learned preprocessing. Keep a separate final evaluation out of this model-selection process.

stages.title: 1. The Validation Set
stages.question: Why can one validation split be noisy?
stages.miniPlan: Split IDs and validation MSE.
stages.interactionPlan: Redraw an explicit development split; rename Test labels to Validation and keep final test separate.
stages.reference: A validation split is a development check, not the final test. Small held-out sets can give noisy rankings. The teaching 50/50 split makes the groups easy to see; it is not a required proportion. Choose splits for sample size, time, groups and deployment conditions.

stages.title: 2. k-Fold Cross-Validation
stages.question: What does K-fold validation average?
stages.miniPlan: Per-fold fit, held-out prediction, score, and mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the folds with distinct fitted models; explain dependence among scores and limits on uncertainty claims.
stages.reference: For five folds, fit on four and validate on the fifth, five times. Learned scaling, imputation and feature selection must be refitted inside every training fold. Average held-out losses with appropriate weighting when fold sizes differ. Overlapping fits are related, so the scores are not independent experiments. Cross-validation gives evidence under a design, not certainty about the future.

stages.title: 3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)
stages.question: What changes in leave-one-out?
stages.miniPlan: One held-out row and almost-overlapping training sets.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a row, inspect its held-out error, and discuss computation and estimator-dependent variance without absolute claims.
stages.reference: With n rows, leave-one-out fits n models and averages n held-out losses. The fits overlap heavily. Its bias, variability and cost depend on the method and population; it is not always better than K-fold. The lab's five-fold selector remains a five-fold illustration, not an implementation of n leave-one-out fits.

stages.title: 4. The Bootstrap
stages.question: What does sampling with replacement mean?
stages.miniPlan: Original IDs and a resample with repeated IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw one bootstrap sample, then many; link duplicate counts to the estimator distribution and interval method.
stages.reference: From 100 rows, draw 100 times while keeping every original row available after each draw. Recalculate the statistic, then repeat. The resulting spread approximates sampling uncertainty under suitable assumptions. It is not fresh independent data and does not repair an unrepresentative sample. Related data need suitable group or time bootstrap methods.

stages.title: Limitations in Practice
stages.question: Which resampling method answers my question?
stages.miniPlan: Model selection / uncertainty / groups / time decision table.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a method for a scenario; include block or cluster resampling where independence fails.
stages.reference: Prediction assessment and estimate uncertainty are different targets. Choose resampling units that reflect independent people, groups, times or locations. An outer evaluation loop can assess an entire selection procedure. Bootstrap and cross-validation are tools with assumptions; neither is a universal best method.

stages.title: Summary & Synthesis
stages.question: Can I distinguish bias, variance, and uncertainty?
stages.miniPlan: Three short scenarios with different sources of error.
stages.interactionPlan: Require an explanation before revealing the method; retain a comparison table for later reference.
stages.reference: Use the definitions rather than personality metaphors about a model being stubborn or distracted. State the input, learning procedure, sample design, loss and what was averaged. Distinguish one fit's errors from repeated-sample behavior, and avoid calling every smooth curve biased or every wiggly curve wrong without evidence.

bias-variance.title: Bias-Variance Trade-Off & Resampling
bias-variance.intro: See why a model can miss a pattern or change too much between samples. Then use fair data splits to compare predictions.
bias-variance.prerequisite: Prediction errors and the difference between training and validation.

stages.title: The Raw Counts
stages.question: Why use counts instead of averages?
stages.miniPlan: Four people allocated to four mutually exclusive cells.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a person and highlight their table cell; distinguish observed counts from percentages.
stages.reference: A category is a label, not an amount to average. One separate example counts 50 students by Art/Sports club and Apples/Chips preference. Each student contributes to one cell. The live notebook may use another example; check its own labels and totals. Use counts for the calculation, although percentages help explain the pattern.

stages.title: Hypotheses & Marginals
stages.question: What does independence predict?
stages.miniPlan: Marginal totals and a common conditional proportion.
stages.interactionPlan: Lock margins and compare tables with different association patterns.
stages.reference: The null model says club and snack are independent in the population. The alternative says they are associated. Row and column totals are called margins. Independence does not require equally sized rows. It requires the same population snack proportions across club categories, after accounting for their sizes.

stages.title: Expected Counts
stages.question: Why multiply row and column totals?
stages.miniPlan: 30 Art students × 25/50 apple share = 15.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight each denominator and margin as the expected cell fills; reveal the other cells only after a prediction.
stages.reference: Expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total. In the separate club example, 30 students are in Art and 25 of all 50 prefer Apples. Expected Art/Apples = 30 × 25/50 = 15. Art/Chips is also 15. The 20-person Sports row has expected counts 10 and 10. Expected is an average under a model; real sample counts need not match it exactly, even when the model is true.

stages.title: Residuals & Contributions
stages.question: Why square and divide by expected count?
stages.miniPlan: Observed → residual → square → contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a cell and link its signed residual with its nonnegative contribution; sum unrounded values.
stages.reference: χ² = Σ[(O − E)²/E]. O is observed, E is expected, and Σ means add across cells. For O = 20 and E = 15, the gap is 5, its square is 25, and 25/15 is about 1.67. The separate club table's four contributions add to about 8.33. Rounded displays may not add exactly; the calculation uses unrounded values. Contributions are not negative and do not show the direction of a gap.

stages.title: The Reference Distribution
stages.question: How unusual is the statistic under independence?
stages.miniPlan: Statistic, df, alpha, and right-tail area.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a hypothetical statistic along the reference curve; replace the claim that chance has been ruled out.
stages.reference: For r rows and c columns, df = (r − 1)(c − 1). A 2×2 table has df 1: once the margins and one cell are fixed, the other cells follow. With df 1, the usual 5% cutoff is about 3.84. A statistic beyond it is evidence against the independence model under the assumptions; it does not rule out chance or prove causation.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.question: What can I conclude from the output?
stages.miniPlan: Evidence / association size / direction / causation, each separate.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the report to residual signs and effect size; mark descriptive size conventions as context dependent.
stages.reference: For observed [20,10;5,15], expected is [15,15;10,10]. N = 50, χ² ≈ 8.333, df = 1, and p ≈ 0.00389. Cramér's V = √(8.333/50) ≈ 0.408. V describes association size; labels such as moderate depend on context. A positive O − E means more than expected; a negative one means fewer. These describe an association, not what caused it.

stages.title: Assumptions & Caveats
stages.question: When is the approximation unsuitable?
stages.miniPlan: Expected counts, independent units, and sparse-table alternatives.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a sparse-count case and choose exact or simulation-based inference where appropriate; keep the original observed data visible.
stages.reference: Use mutually exclusive categories and observations appropriate for the independence model. Several visits from one person are not several independent people. The usual chi-square reference can work poorly with small expected counts. Fisher's exact test is an option for sparse 2×2 tables; larger tables may need other exact or simulation methods. Yates' correction is specific to 2×2 tables and does not guarantee sparse-data reliability. State the counts, method, assumptions, effect size and pattern without a causal claim.

chi-square.title: Chi-Square Test of Independence
chi-square.intro: Count how often two categories appear together. Compare the real counts with the counts expected if the categories were unrelated.
chi-square.prerequisite: Fractions, percentages, and reading a small table.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What is the target category?
stages.miniPlan: One labeled observation with its features.
stages.interactionPlan: Link row and point; give classes text/shape identities before coloring regions.
stages.reference: The labels are known answers for training rows. Inputs are the measurements used to predict them. The root holds all training rows; a split creates two children; a leaf is a group that stops splitting. The live dot plot and tree diagram show the same selected point and fitted rules.

stages.title: Split rows into training, validation and final test
stages.question: Which rows may choose a split?
stages.miniPlan: Train/validation/test role strip.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep test labels sealed during depth and pruning comparisons.
stages.reference: Test data must not choose cutoffs, depth, leaf size, pruning or input preparation. The live display uses validation while controls change. Separate final-test rows remain sealed. The small printed example and live dataset are separate. Read each sample size when you check a calculation.

stages.title: The Root Node
stages.question: What does the root predict before splitting?
stages.miniPlan: Class counts and majority baseline.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a class count and show the corresponding observations.
stages.reference: If the root has 6 class-1 rows and 4 class-0 rows, its class-1 fraction is 6/10=.6. The usual .5 decision cutoff chooses class 1. That fraction describes training membership. It is not a guarantee that the next point belongs to class 1.

stages.title: Measuring Messiness
stages.question: What is impurity?
stages.miniPlan: Two tiny class mixtures and their Gini calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust a toy proportion; contrast pure, mixed, and maximum-impurity nodes.
stages.reference: For several classes, Gini = 1−Σp_i²; Σ means add across classes. Binary .5 is the maximum only for two equally likely classes. Entropy is another criterion; binary entropy with base-2 logs reaches 1 for an even mix. Both measure mixture, but may choose different cuts. Low impurity is not itself evidence that the features cause the labels.

stages.title: Testing Every Question
stages.question: Why inspect several candidate questions?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate feature/threshold list.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a threshold over valid candidate positions; preserve the same parent node.
stages.reference: For a numeric input, this lab sorts distinct training values and tests their midpoints. It evaluates valid questions using weighted child impurity. Different software can use other implementations, but the candidate question must separate training rows according to its stated comparison rule.

stages.title: How the Tree Scores One Split
stages.question: How is split improvement calculated?
stages.miniPlan: Parent impurity minus weighted child impurities.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal child weights and contributions; show why an unweighted average can choose the wrong split.
stages.reference: For child sizes n_L and n_R, weighted impurity = (n_L/n)Gini_L+(n_R/n)Gini_R. Gain subtracts this from parent impurity. Weighting avoids counting a one-row child as much as a large child. The chosen cut is locally best among allowed candidates, not an absolute best tree across all future choices.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.question: How is the procedure reused in a child?
stages.miniPlan: The split recipe copied into one branch.
stages.interactionPlan: Expand one selected node and its corresponding region in feature space.
stages.reference: Reuse the same search inside a child rather than applying a child's cut to unrelated regions. Stop for purity, maximum depth, insufficient rows, leaf-size requirements or inadequate gain. These conditions are configurable limits. Pure training leaves do not prove future predictions are perfect.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.question: Why do tree boundaries look rectangular?
stages.miniPlan: One feature threshold extended into a region.
stages.interactionPlan: Link successive tree questions to axis-aligned partitions without moving the underlying points.
stages.reference: A leaf's class fraction is class count/leaf count. A leaf containing one positive row gives 100% locally, but that is very little evidence about future rows. Probability calibration and minimum leaf size matter. Axis-aligned cuts can represent curves through many steps, not through a guaranteed smooth boundary.

stages.title: Depth Limiting vs. Post-Pruning
stages.question: How do depth limits and pruning differ?
stages.miniPlan: Stop-growing rule versus cut-back subtree.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare both on a fixed full tree; show the selected leaves and validation consequences.
stages.reference: The pruning lab starts with a fixed depth-5 tree and removes branches as the penalty rises. This is different from reducing maximum depth and fitting a fresh early-stopped tree. Compare retained leaves, training risk and validation performance to see the actual tradeoff.

stages.title: Choosing Tree Depth
stages.question: How should we select tree depth?
stages.miniPlan: Training and validation curve with selected candidate.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub depth with fixed splits; keep final-test accuracy unavailable during selection.
stages.reference: Training accuracy and validation accuracy answer different questions. A measured validation curve may be noisy or flat; do not assume the best depth is always 3. Select a useful, stable setting using development data, then freeze it before final evaluation.

stages.title: Classify new validation points
stages.question: How does one new row travel through the tree?
stages.miniPlan: A yes/no decision receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace the query across nodes and spatial regions; display equality rules and missing-value policy.
stages.reference: This lab sends equality to the left branch. Follow the query's actual x₁ or x₂ value at each question. The highlighted map region and tree route must reach the same leaf. Saved training counts give the class fraction; the query's unknown label does not enter that calculation.

stages.title: Performance Metrics
stages.question: Which errors does the tree make?
stages.miniPlan: Confusion matrix with actual/predicted definitions.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a cell to reveal member rows; derive all rates from the same counts.
stages.reference: Define the positive class. FP predicts positive for an actual negative; FN predicts negative for an actual positive. Precision divides by predicted positives; recall divides by actual positives. Report counts and sample sizes, especially for rare classes. Changing the model during this display is development, not repeated final testing.

stages.title: Reading Tree Output
stages.question: What belongs in tree output?
stages.miniPlan: Node rule, n, impurity, class distribution, prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Link each output row to its node and region; keep confidence claims qualified.
stages.reference: State the target labels, inputs, split structure, criterion, maximum depth, minimum leaf size, pruning and threshold. Include validation or final-test roles accurately, error measures, uncertainty and limits. A path explains how the fitted prediction was produced, not how changing an input would cause a real-world outcome.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: What changes when I modify complexity?
stages.miniPlan: Saved baseline versus current tree summary.
stages.interactionPlan: Explore depth/leaf size with preserved seed and validation data; allow replay of one prediction path.
stages.reference: Keep the sample fixed while changing one constraint. That isolates the setting's effect on cuts and leaves. Drawing a new dataset changes a second cause. Inspect whether better training fit also improves useful errors outside training.

stages.title: Limitations & Model Choice
stages.question: When should I prefer another model?
stages.miniPlan: Instability, interaction capacity, axis alignment, and ensemble options.
stages.interactionPlan: Perturb one training case and compare the tree; explain tradeoffs rather than declaring a universal winner.
stages.reference: Numeric threshold trees usually do not need rescaling merely because input units differ; they compare values within one feature at a time. Native categorical support depends on software, so some inputs need encoding. Trees can be sensitive to data changes, rare classes and many small leaves. A forest still has piecewise tree-based predictions; averaging does not guarantee a smooth function or calibrated probabilities. Compare alternatives for the actual goal.

classification-trees.title: Classification Trees
classification-trees.intro: Use input questions to divide labelled examples into groups. Follow a new point to the leaf that gives its class prediction.
classification-trees.prerequisite: Fractions, two-axis plots, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: What uncertainty does an estimate leave?
stages.miniPlan: Point estimate and plausible values under a stated model.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare two samples with the same estimated effect but different precision.
stages.reference: An estimate might be 4 points in both studies. If study A has SE 1 and study B has SE 3, A's interval is narrower under the same method. The interval width describes precision. Decide what size of change would matter before using the interval to judge practical value.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What do a confidence interval and a p-value ask?
stages.miniPlan: Repeated-procedure coverage versus tail probability under H₀.
stages.interactionPlan: Select one question and highlight its reference distribution; avoid posterior-probability interpretations.
stages.reference: A 95% confidence method covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated uses under its assumptions. Once this interval is calculated, the parameter is not randomly moving around inside it. For the usual frequentist interval, do not call 95% the probability that this fixed parameter lies in this specific interval. The p-value assumes the null and asks about results at least as extreme.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How do we compute one interval and test?
stages.miniPlan: Effect, SE, statistic, tail area, interval endpoints.
stages.interactionPlan: Step a fully stated toy model; put assumptions and approximation labels beside the numbers.
stages.reference: In the receipt, the estimate is 4, known SD is 10 and n is 100. SE = 10/10 = 1. The interval is 4 ± 1.96 = [2.04,5.96]. For null 0, z = (4−0)/1 = 4. A separate example with interval [1,7] and p = .01 illustrates reporting; it is not this calculation. A p-value .01 is not a 1% chance that the null is true.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do alpha, beta, power, and effect size connect?
stages.miniPlan: A true-null/false-null decision table.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare null and specified alternative distributions; power is prospective for an alternative, not observed truth probability.
stages.reference: A Type I error rejects a true null; alpha controls its rate under the assumptions. A Type II error misses a specific alternative; beta is its probability. Power = 1−beta. Lowering alpha usually lowers power if everything else stays the same. Family-wise control limits the chance of any false rejection in a family; false-discovery-rate control targets the expected proportion of false discoveries. These are different goals. Neither automatically repairs outcome switching or unplanned stopping.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: Why does larger n change precision?
stages.miniPlan: Fixed effect with two SE values.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust n/effect with dynamic chart domains so extreme intervals remain visible; keep units and reference model explicit.
stages.reference: For SD 10, n 25 gives SE 2 and n 100 gives SE 1. Sample size affects precision, not the definition of practical importance. Set a meaningful effect size for the application, then compare the estimate and interval with it.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: When can the nominal result mislead?
stages.miniPlan: Dependence, optional stopping, multiplicity, and model failure.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a failure scenario and inspect which inference condition breaks.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

The estimator, test and sampling design must fit the question. Stated error rates rely on their model assumptions and a suitable plan for repeated comparisons.

When the method fails

Dependence means some observations share information. Multiple testing means many opportunities for a small p-value. Optional stopping means repeatedly checking and stopping by an unplanned rule. Each issue needs its own suitable design or analysis. A multiple-testing adjustment does not fix wrongly treating related rows as independent.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: What should be decided before looking at results?
stages.miniPlan: Question → meaningful effect → design → analysis plan → data.
stages.interactionPlan: Arrange the analysis sequence and explain corrections for a prespecified family of tests.
stages.reference: Name the quantity you want to estimate, called the estimand. Specify H₀, the null, and H₁, the alternative. Choose alpha, outcomes, model, data collection and any comparison adjustment before seeing results. If you explore after seeing the data, say so and use suitable follow-up validation.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: How do we report a result without overclaiming?
stages.miniPlan: Estimate + interval + model + p + practical importance.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare two drafted conclusions; distinguish lack of evidence from evidence of negligible effect.
stages.reference: What to report: Give the estimate in meaningful units, uncertainty interval, sample size, method, assumptions and any multiple-comparison plan. A wide interval containing zero can also contain worthwhile effects. To show an effect is small enough to count as equivalent, define an equivalence margin and use an appropriate planned analysis.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I interpret uncertainty correctly?
stages.miniPlan: A new interval/p-value pair and a sentence completion.
stages.interactionPlan: Use misconception-specific feedback and nonfixed answer positions; retain deeper explanations.
stages.reference: Compare the interval with both zero and the practical threshold. A very narrow interval far below that threshold may show a real but unimportant change. A wide interval can leave important uncertainty even when the point estimate looks large. Explain that uncertainty instead of treating p < .05 as proof.

confidence-hypothesis-testing.title: Confidence Intervals & Hypothesis Testing
confidence-hypothesis-testing.intro: An estimate is not the whole story. Learn to read an uncertainty range and a p-value without claiming more than the data supports.
confidence-hypothesis-testing.prerequisite: Averages, fractions, and standard error from Probability & Sampling.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What makes observations paired?
stages.miniPlan: One student's two measurements and units.
stages.interactionPlan: Link a table row to its point; intentionally swap a pair to show why row identity matters.
stages.reference: Hours and score must come from the same student. Sorting the columns separately creates pairs that nobody observed. The separate reference example has students A–F with hours 1–6 and scores 52,57,63,68,74,79. Its table is separate from the live notebook. The live dots follow its current selected dataset.

stages.title: Direction and Form
stages.question: What do direction and form tell us?
stages.miniPlan: Positive, negative, and curved mini scatterplots.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a pattern while preserving axes; name linear versus non-linear association before showing r.
stages.reference: Dots rising from left to right suggest positive association. Dots falling suggest negative association. Always check curves, separate groups and unusual points too. A curve can be clear even when a straight-line number gives a weak summary.

stages.title: Measuring Strength: r
stages.question: What does r measure?
stages.miniPlan: Sign versus magnitude in two short rows.
stages.interactionPlan: Change noise with the same underlying points; keep slope and r conceptually distinct.
stages.reference: r = +1 means all varying pairs fall on an increasing straight line. r = −1 means they fall on a decreasing straight line. r = 0 means no linear association in these pairs. It does not exclude curved relationships. The calculation divides covariance, a measure of shared movement, by the two standard deviations. Both measurements need nonzero spread for r to be defined.

stages.title: Formal Hypotheses
stages.question: What is the null about?
stages.miniPlan: Sample r versus population rho.
stages.interactionPlan: Predict whether a sample can have nonzero r when population rho is zero; replace the significant-alternative wording.
stages.reference: ρ, pronounced rho, names population correlation. r names the sample estimate. H₀: ρ = 0 is the null model; H₁: ρ ≠ 0 is the alternative. The alternative says correlation is nonzero, not automatically statistically significant. The usual t statistic is r√((n − 2)/(1 − r²)); its test needs independent pairs and suitable distributional assumptions. Failure to reject does not prove independence.

stages.title: How it works: Covariability
stages.question: Why multiply deviations from the means?
stages.miniPlan: One row with x−mean(x), y−mean(y), and their product.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush each quadrant and accumulate signed contributions; link the denominator to scaling rather than unexplained normalization.
stages.reference: The symbol Σ means add across all pairs. A bar over a letter means its average. A positive gap times a positive gap is positive; two negative gaps also give a positive product. For gaps +2 and −3, the product is −6. The bottom of the r formula scales the total using each measurement's spread, making r free of units.

stages.title: Assumptions: Paired & Linear
stages.question: Can r miss a strong pattern?
stages.miniPlan: A straight cloud versus a U-shaped cloud.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle the U-shape and reveal near-zero r; do not call this absence of all dependence.
stages.reference: Pearson r can be calculated for numeric pairs even when the pattern is curved; the problem is interpreting that number as the whole relationship. Spearman describes a pattern that keeps rising or keeps falling, even if it curves. Such a pattern is called monotonic. It can also miss a U-shape because a U-shape changes direction.

stages.title: Robustness Check: Outliers
stages.question: Why can one point change r so much?
stages.miniPlan: Before/after r with the outlier's contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Move one selected point using drag or numeric inputs; retain a ghost of its original location.
stages.reference: Outliers are unusual values. Influential points are ones that change the answer a lot; these are related but different ideas. Check measurements and study context. A far-away point affects the averages and the products used in covariance. Report a justified sensitivity comparison instead of choosing the version that looks strongest.

stages.title: The Inferential Result
stages.question: What does the test result mean?
stages.miniPlan: r, interval, n, p, and their distinct questions.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through the null reference and report; define inference assumptions separately from calculating descriptive r.
stages.reference: A p-value is calculated assuming the null model and test assumptions. It concerns a result at least this extreme, not the probability that chance caused the result. Report the sample size, r, an appropriate interval, shape and data collection method. Practical importance depends on the application, not only on crossing p = 0.05.

stages.title: The Golden Rule: Causation
stages.question: Why does association not establish cause?
stages.miniPlan: A three-node common-cause sketch.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal temperature as a shared cause of two measures; require an association-only conclusion.
stages.reference: A confounder is another cause linked to both quantities. Hot weather can raise ice-cream sales and swimming, creating an association without ice cream causing drowning. Selection can also create links. Adjusting for one measured factor does not guarantee all hidden causes have been handled. Cause-and-effect conclusions require a suitable design and assumptions.
stages.experiment: Trace both arrows from hot weather. Explain how swimming and ice-cream sales could rise together without one causing the other. What additional evidence would distinguish possible explanations?

stages.title: Limitations & Summary
stages.question: Which correlation should I use?
stages.miniPlan: Pearson / Spearman / neither, with conditions.
stages.interactionPlan: Classify linear, monotonic curved, and U-shaped examples; give corrective feedback rather than a blanket switch rule.
stages.reference: Changing metres to centimetres keeps r the same because it is a positive linear change of units. Pearson summarizes numeric linear association. Spearman compares ranks, while Kendall compares agreement in pair ordering. Neither rank measure automatically fixes unusual data, related observations, hidden causes or patterns that change direction. Plot the pairs and explain why the chosen measure suits the question.

correlation.title: Correlation
correlation.intro: Do two measurements tend to rise or fall together? Start with dots, then learn what one correlation number can and cannot tell us.
correlation.prerequisite: Averages and reading a plot with two axes.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: How can a good score be misleading?
stages.miniPlan: A feature available before versus after the outcome.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the timing of each feature and identify an unavailable-at-prediction clue.
stages.reference: Prediction time is the moment the model must decide. A clue recorded after the outcome, such as a later billing code, may reveal the answer without being available then. A score using that clue evaluates a procedure we cannot actually use at the intended time.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What information is allowed to cross a split?
stages.miniPlan: Fit on train; transform held-out rows with frozen parameters.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a scaler statistic across a pipeline and expose an intentionally leaked version.
stages.reference: The pipeline includes everything that learns from data, not only the final classifier. Means, missing-value fills, category frequencies, selected inputs, PCA directions, oversampling rules and thresholds can all carry information. Fit them within the relevant training or development boundary. An untouched outer evaluation must stay outside every such choice.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: What does leakage change in a concrete example?
stages.miniPlan: Safe versus leaked workflow with identical split IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare an explicitly computed toy example or labeled schematic; explain why score inflation is not a fixed amount.
stages.reference: For 1,000 rows in five equal folds, each turn has 800 training and 200 validation rows. If we fill missing ages with the mean of all 1,000 first, every validation group helps set its own fill. Instead fit five training-only imputers, one for each turn, then apply each to its 200 held-out rows.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: What kinds of leakage exist?
stages.miniPlan: Features, duplicate rows, groups, time, and repeated selection.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect one case per type; replace the repeated generic paragraph with specific causal paths.
stages.reference: Duplicate images across folds leak row information. Repeated people may leak identity. A rolling feature using future values leaks time. Repeatedly choosing from final-test scores leaks selection information. Target encoding needs cross-fitting so a training row's own target does not create its encoded input. Correct software order still needs the right groups, times and deployment question.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: Can I repair this pipeline?
stages.miniPlan: Current ordering of split, imputation, scaling, selection, fit, score.
stages.interactionPlan: Select/move steps using buttons as well as drag; show exactly which fit call crossed the boundary.
stages.reference: fit means learn parameters from the training part. transform means apply those learned parameters to another part. Do not fit a separate validation scaler or use validation labels to choose missing-value fills. A prediction should be made before its held-out outcome is used for scoring.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can pipelines fail to prevent?
stages.miniPlan: Bad timestamps, target proxies, wrong groups, and changing availability.
stages.interactionPlan: Show an operationally impossible feature that remains invalid despite correct software ordering.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

The split must match prediction time and the independent unit. Each input must exist when a decision is made. Learned preparation must stay inside training.

When the method fails

Trace source dates, measurement availability, duplicates and related groups. Random row folds may be unsuitable for forecasting or prediction for new people or organizations. A pipeline protects its declared boundaries; it cannot decide the right independent unit on its own.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should nested selection work?
stages.miniPlan: Outer evaluation around an inner tuning loop.
stages.interactionPlan: Step one outer fold and reveal refitted inner transforms; preserve group/time constraints.
stages.reference: For each outer split, reserve its evaluation rows. On the remaining rows, fit and compare candidates using inner folds. Refit the selected procedure on the outer training portion, then predict the untouched outer rows. This assesses a selection method, rather than just one candidate's favorable inner score.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: How do I document a defensible pipeline?
stages.miniPlan: Feature availability, split unit, fitted steps, and sealed test.
stages.interactionPlan: Produce a compact provenance checklist from concrete choices.
stages.reference: What to report: Record the task, input availability, identifiers or reproducible split rules, group/time structure, pipeline order and target-aware transformations. Save the rules needed to repeat predictions. Keep evaluation roles visible so a validation score is not presented as an independent final-test result.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I spot a new leakage path?
stages.miniPlan: One unfamiliar grouped/time-dependent scenario.
stages.interactionPlan: Ask which information crossed the boundary and how to repair it; give specific feedback for the chosen misconception.
stages.reference: Ask whether this value or analyst decision could know anything it was meant to be evaluated against. Check learned statistics as well as labels. Fix the earliest inappropriate information path, rerun development evaluation, and obtain fresh final evidence if the previous test helped make new choices.

data-leakage-pipelines.title: Data Leakage & Pipelines
data-leakage-pipelines.intro: Check what information a prediction was allowed to know. Keep every learned preparation step inside the right training boundary.
data-leakage-pipelines.prerequisite: The roles of training, validation and final-test data.

stages.title: Define the finish line
stages.question: What exactly should the system output?
stages.miniPlan: Classify / locate / segment, with one input image.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep the image stable while outputs change; explain that example scores are illustrative.
stages.reference: Keep the apple image fixed while comparing an image label, a location box and a pixel mask. These are distinct outputs, not different accuracy scores for one identical task. Define a realistic input, target and success measure before choosing architecture. The lab's small illustrative task outputs are not predictions from a trained image model.

stages.title: Collect reality, not shortcuts
stages.question: What shortcut might the model learn?
stages.miniPlan: Animal label versus background, with counterexamples.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a suspicious cue and reveal a counterexample; connect data collection choices to failure modes.
stages.reference: In a background-shortcut example, changing scenery can change a rule's answer even though the apple remains the same. The rule demonstrates a failure mechanism. It does not diagnose every network. Collect useful variation, inspect sources and duplicates, and test plausible counterexamples. More copies of one narrow situation do not add broad coverage.

stages.title: Split before you tune
stages.question: Which examples may influence which choices?
stages.miniPlan: Training weights / validation choices / sealed final test.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a duplicate or related-source group into an intentionally wrong split, then repair it with keyboard controls.
stages.reference: Choose the independent unit and prediction timing. Keep related images, videos, people or devices together as the task requires. Learn any normalization or preparation on training data. Use validation for design and checkpoint selection, and reserve a suitable final test. A 70/15/15 split is one example, not a universal requirement.

stages.title: Turn examples into tensors
stages.question: What is a tensor's shape?
stages.miniPlan: One image channel, token ID, embedding row, or audio window.
stages.interactionPlan: Follow one input through the chosen representation; avoid implying token IDs have numeric semantic distances.
stages.reference: The live grayscale patch is 5×5, so it contains 25 numbers. Eight such examples form a batch of 200 numbers. A colour image also has channels. Text tokenization splits text into pieces with IDs; an embedding maps an ID to a learned vector. Audio can use sampled amplitudes or frequency summaries over time. Preserve the declared order, dimensions and preparation at prediction time.

stages.title: Inside one neuron
stages.question: What does one neuron do?
stages.miniPlan: x·w terms, bias, sum, activation.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one weight and trace a computed result; synchronize the left receipt and right neuron.
stages.reference: For one neuron, add weight×input products and the bias, then transform the sum. The bias is a starting offset. ReLU takes the larger of zero and the sum. A negative product is not automatically an absent input; it lowers the total. The diagram's products, sum and response must refer to the same selected values.

stages.title: Depth builds features
stages.question: Why might depth help?
stages.miniPlan: Local pattern → composition → task-useful feature.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through a labeled illustrative hierarchy; explain that every network need not learn literal ears or eyes.
stages.reference: A convolution filter multiplies a local input window by its weights and adds the products. Reusing it across positions creates a feature map. The shown edge filters are explicit teaching filters, not learned evidence that a network recognized an object. Real training learns filter values from its objective. Deeper layers compose responses; their human descriptions are helpful interpretations, not guaranteed roles.

stages.title: How learning happens
stages.question: How does the correction cycle work?
stages.miniPlan: Forward/loss/backprop/update with one numeric parameter.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep marks persistent across phases; gradients appear before weights change; provide pause and rewind.
stages.reference: Forward uses the current parameters to make predictions. Loss compares them with targets. Backpropagation uses the chain rule to compute local slopes. The optimizer applies a step, with learning rate controlling its size. The gradient points uphill; its negative points locally downhill. A large step can make loss worse. One local diagram does not show every parameter of a large model.

stages.title: Learn patterns, not the answer sheet
stages.question: How do we reduce overfitting?
stages.miniPlan: Method / what changes / when used / tradeoff.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare dropout training/evaluation, augmentation, weight decay, and early stopping as distinct interventions.
stages.reference: Dropout changes training computation and is disabled for ordinary evaluation, with the method's scaling handled consistently. The lab's fixed mask illustrates one comparison, not random dropout over a complete training run. Augmentation should preserve the target meaning. Weight decay and early stopping are different mechanisms; none is universally required or guaranteed to help. Choose them using development evidence.

stages.title: Choose an architecture
stages.question: Why choose CNN, RNN, or attention?
stages.miniPlan: Locality / sequential state / pairwise context comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Give each architecture a readable subscene and one traceable input; avoid fitting all mechanisms into miniature labels.
stages.reference: A CNN reuses learned filters across positions; it does not create a new filter for every image. An RNN passes a fixed-length state from one step to the next. Attention makes query–key scores, normalizes them into weights, then sums weighted values into context. Standard full attention can need memory growing quadratically with sequence length. These local diagrams expose mechanics, not a measured ranking of whole architectures.

stages.title: Start from a pretrained model
stages.question: What is reused during transfer learning?
stages.miniPlan: Frozen backbone, new head, then selected unfrozen layers.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle trainable regions with clear parameter labels; show the exact adaptation sequence and domain-mismatch caveat.
stages.reference: The backbone supplies reused features; the head maps them to the new target. Freeze means do not update those parameters. In this lab early features remain frozen, while a later backbone section may be trainable and the new head is trainable in both settings. Fine-tuning can adapt useful features, but source-data bias or a mismatched target can still hurt. Validate rather than assuming transfer is beneficial.

stages.title: Make an honest judgement
stages.question: What would make an evaluation honest and useful?
stages.miniPlan: Per-class counts, calibration, subgroup slices, chosen threshold.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect errors after a locked choice; label subsequent model revisions as needing fresh evaluation.
stages.reference: Choose thresholds and checkpoints on validation, then evaluate the completed procedure independently. Report per-class counts and useful metrics, uncertainty, calibration and relevant subgroup results. Inspect errors for bad labels or shortcuts. The live scene keeps final-test labels sealed and uses validation. High average accuracy can still hide systematic misses.

stages.title: Ship the whole pipeline
stages.question: What does deployment actually package?
stages.miniPlan: Input contract → transforms → model → decision → monitoring.
stages.interactionPlan: Break one contract deliberately and repair it; show drift monitoring without implying drift alone proves failure.
stages.reference: Save the architecture, weights, class order, input names, shapes, normalization, vocabulary or sample-rate rules, and decision policy. Use the correct evaluation mode and handle invalid inputs explicitly. Test the complete path in its target environment for resource use and failures. A deployed model can require different practical tradeoffs than the same model in a notebook.

deep-learning.title: Deep Learning
deep-learning.intro: Choose an output, represent the input as numbers, and follow the local calculations that larger networks repeat.
deep-learning.prerequisite: Neural Networks, multiplication, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: What causal comparison do we want?
stages.miniPlan: Population, treatment, comparator, outcome, time.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a concrete estimand before choosing a statistical test.
stages.reference: The estimand is the specific quantity we want to learn. For example, average score difference after one term between two assigned teaching strategies in eligible schools. A sophisticated test cannot repair a design that never collected the needed comparison. Distinguish the chosen population and strategy from a vague claim that something works.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What does random assignment accomplish?
stages.miniPlan: Confounder balance in expectation versus one realized allocation.
stages.interactionPlan: Randomize repeatedly and show finite-sample imbalance; separate assignment from random sampling.
stages.reference: A confounder is a factor associated with both treatment and outcome. Random assignment avoids deliberately choosing treatment based on those factors and balances them in expectation. It does not guarantee exact balance in this sample. Random sampling concerns population representation, so a randomized treatment study can still use a nonrepresentative volunteer sample.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: Why are twenty schools not six hundred independent assignments?
stages.miniPlan: School clusters with student members.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an assignment unit and highlight all its students; keep the independent unit explicit.
stages.reference: Twenty schools assigned with 30 students each produce 600 measurements, but only 20 assignment units. Outcomes within schools may be correlated. Analyze and plan precision for that group structure rather than pretending each student received an independent random assignment. The needed method depends on the design and target.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do blocking, blinding, and intention-to-treat differ?
stages.miniPlan: Design choice / threat addressed / what it does not fix.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace one participant from assignment through analysis; retain noncompliance and interference caveats.
stages.reference: Allocation concealment prevents knowing the next assignment during enrollment. Blinding reduces changes in behavior or measurement from knowing assignment. Blocking randomizes within relevant similar groups. Intention-to-treat compares assigned strategies, including imperfect adherence; per-protocol comparison concerns those who followed the protocol and can be more sensitive to selection. Plan missingness, spillover and adherence before results are known.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: How does clustering affect effective information?
stages.miniPlan: Design effect 1+(m−1)ICC and n/design effect.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust n, cluster size, and ICC; label approximation assumptions and replace the ad hoc power formula before presenting it as calculated power.
stages.reference: For group size m and within-group correlation ICC, design effect ≈1+(m−1)ICC. For m=30 and ICC=.05, it is 2.45; 600/2.45≈245 is a rough information comparison. The formula has assumptions and does not replace power planning. Number of groups, unequal sizes, allocation, variance, effect, missingness and analysis method also matter. The lab illustrates this formula only.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can break a randomized comparison?
stages.miniPlan: Attrition, spillover, noncompliance, and outcome switching.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a failure and show the broken comparison; do not suggest randomization cures every later bias.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Assignment, measurement and follow-up must support the intended comparison. Account for related groups, interference, nonadherence and missing outcomes where relevant.

When the method fails

Attrition means missing follow-up outcomes. Noncompliance means not following assignment. Interference or spillover means one unit's treatment affects another's outcome. Differential losses or changing the outcome after seeing results can undermine the intended comparison. State what was observed and the assumptions needed for the resulting effect estimate.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: What should be planned before recruitment?
stages.miniPlan: Estimand, unit, allocation, power, outcomes, analysis, missingness.
stages.interactionPlan: Build the protocol in causal order; include plausible attrition and number of clusters.
stages.reference: Prespecify the main outcome, timing, effect contrast, randomization unit, concealment, blocks, analysis and comparison adjustments. Sample-size or power calculations need a meaningful alternative, plausible variance, allocation, group structure and expected missingness. Test sensitivity to those assumptions. The design-effect lab does not itself calculate complete study power.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What belongs in a transparent report?
stages.miniPlan: Allocation, exclusions, adherence, effect/interval, harms, deviations.
stages.interactionPlan: Fill a short report and identify a missing design fact.
stages.reference: What to report: Give the protocol and deviations, randomization and concealment, units, exclusions, follow-up completeness, adherence and relevant harms. Report effects in meaningful units with uncertainty, not only a p-value. Explain primary and secondary comparisons and any multiple-testing plan.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I identify the unit and analysis implication?
stages.miniPlan: A new clinic/classroom randomization scenario.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose the independent unit and explain why row count is insufficient; retain static feedback.
stages.reference: If classrooms are assigned, keep that unit visible even when outcomes are measured on pupils. Repeated measurements can add another dependence layer. A suitable analysis handles the assignment contrast and the related outcomes. Random assignment does not justify ignoring how observations are linked.

experimental-design.title: Experimental Design & Randomisation
experimental-design.intro: Choose the comparison before collecting the data. See what random assignment does, and why the unit being assigned matters.
experimental-design.prerequisite: Averages, uncertainty, and the difference between association and cause.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why add another learner to the current model?
stages.miniPlan: Current prediction, error, proposed correction.
stages.interactionPlan: Show a weak learner contributing a small improvement rather than replacing the ensemble.
stages.reference: Unlike an independently averaged forest, boosting fits an ordered sequence. A weak learner is a simple model contributing one correction. It need not be wrong or unhelpful by itself. Each learner depends on the predictions made by the earlier ensemble.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What is learned at the next round?
stages.miniPlan: Negative loss gradient; squared-error residual as a special case.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight targets for a new learner under squared loss, then explain why other losses differ.
stages.reference: A gradient tells how loss changes as the prediction changes. Its negative points towards a smaller loss locally. Under squared loss, that direction is proportional to the residual. Other losses use different pseudo-residuals, meaning targets computed from their gradients. Do not assume every boosting algorithm fits ordinary raw residuals.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How do three rounds build a prediction?
stages.miniPlan: Initial prediction + learning-rate-scaled corrections.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the additive calculation with actual values and a consistent selected row.
stages.reference: In a separate example, start at F₀=10. Three learners output 4,−1,2 at the same point. With rate .2, prediction is 10+.2(4−1+2)=11. These outputs illustrate addition. In real fitting, each later tree is trained after previous corrections; changing the rate generally requires fitting the sequence again.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Why do learning rate and round count interact?
stages.miniPlan: Few large steps versus many small contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare trajectories with fixed training data; explain that their product alone is not a complete equivalence.
stages.reference: Learning rate scales each contribution; depth controls a learner's allowed interactions; rounds control how many learners are added. Row or feature subsampling can also affect fitting. Their effects interact. Equal products of rate and round count do not imply identical models because the subsequent targets change.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: When should we stop adding rounds?
stages.miniPlan: Train/validation loss and the selected checkpoint.
stages.interactionPlan: Use computed or visibly illustrative curves; fix vertical orientation, label axes, and freeze final-test data.
stages.reference: Validation-based early stopping is a model-selection choice. Keep it out of the final test. The curve may be flat or irregular, and a tiny minimum may be uncertain. Choose a useful checkpoint under a stated rule, not the round with the lowest final-test loss.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can a complex boosted model still get wrong?
stages.miniPlan: Overfit, leakage, miscalibration, and shifted data.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a failure case and compare regularization options without presenting gain importance as causality.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

The loss must match the prediction task. Input preparation, tuning and early stopping must stay within development data, with evaluation suited to deployment.

When the method fails

More rounds can chase sample-specific noise. Class weights change the loss objective and may affect probability calibration. Feature-gain or attribution scores describe the fitted procedure, not a causal mechanism. Related inputs can affect how importance is distributed. Assess later data and the relevant population.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should tuning be organized?
stages.miniPlan: Rate, depth, rounds, subsampling, validation.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one setting, refit on train, choose on validation; use cancellation for obsolete computations.
stages.reference: Choose the objective and baseline, then use a suitable validation design for the task. Fit preparation inside development folds. Tune interacting settings together, with a planned search and stopping rule. Compare subgroup errors, calibration where relevant, runtime and uncertainty.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What do we report about the selected ensemble?
stages.miniPlan: Loss, validation strategy, stopping round, parameters, baseline, limitations.
stages.interactionPlan: Produce a compact model record and explain why training loss did not select the final round.
stages.reference: What to report: State the implementation and objective, learning rate, tree constraints, selected round, any subsampling and the checkpoint rule. Report training versus validation roles accurately and evaluate a locked procedure on suitable final data. Do not choose the number of trees from the final-test minimum.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I compute the next prediction?
stages.miniPlan: Initial 10 plus a learner's correction scaled by eta.
stages.interactionPlan: Complete one update and identify when residual fitting is valid; explain the distractors.
stages.reference: For squared-loss teaching, residual = actual−current prediction. A learner fits those residual targets; its output is multiplied by the learning rate. New prediction = current + rate×learner output. The new residual uses the updated total, not just the last learner by itself.

gradient-boosting.title: Gradient Boosting
gradient-boosting.intro: Build a prediction through small corrections. Follow what each new learner adds to the answer already there.
gradient-boosting.prerequisite: Regression trees, prediction errors, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: The Uncharted Planet
stages.question: What does grouping without an answer key mean?
stages.miniPlan: Two reasonable partitions of the same objects.
stages.interactionPlan: Select the feature representation first; avoid claiming there is one natural grouping waiting to be discovered.
stages.reference: Unsupervised means the grouping is not trained against an answer label. A cluster is a group made by the selected distance and linkage. There may be several useful groupings, or no meaningful grouping for the task. Do not promise that the algorithm discovers one hidden true set of categories.

stages.title: Measuring "Close"
stages.question: How do we define close?
stages.miniPlan: One distance calculation with x/y contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Link a distance-matrix cell to two points; compare Euclidean and an appropriate alternative.
stages.reference: Euclidean distance is straight-line distance in the chosen coordinates. Other options include Manhattan, cosine-related or domain-specific measures. Scaling can change which pair is nearest. Choose it according to units and the purpose; automatic standardization is not always desirable. For deployment or validation tasks, any learned preparation needs an appropriate fitting boundary.
stages.experiment: Choose an observation and compare it with its nearest other point. Check the two axis gaps and their straight-line distance. Change the z units and see whether the nearest point changes.

stages.title: The First Merge
stages.question: Why merge this pair first?
stages.miniPlan: Sorted candidate distances with a tie policy.
stages.interactionPlan: Predict the closest pair, then merge while preserving member identities.
stages.reference: The smallest eligible pairwise value gives the first merge. If several pairs tie, a fixed implementation rule chooses their order. The next merge is chosen using updated group distances, not simply the next original point-to-point distance.

stages.title: Defining Group Distance (Linkage)
stages.question: How far apart are groups?
stages.miniPlan: Single / complete / average / Ward definitions.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight contributing pairs and recompute the selected linkage; label Ward's increase-in-variance meaning.
stages.reference: Point distance and group linkage are different choices. Single linkage can form chains; complete often favors compact groups. Ward is tied to Euclidean squared geometry and minimizes an increase in within-cluster spread. Dendrogram height does not mean the same mathematical quantity for every linkage, so label the method and scale.
stages.experiment: Set Merge steps to 3, then compare linkage rules. The picture zooms in on the next two groups and marks the distances used by the rule. Each rule may create a different merge history from the same eight observations.

stages.title: The Process in Motion
stages.question: How is the merge history built?
stages.miniPlan: Before/after group membership for one merge.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub cached merge snapshots in both directions; synchronize point clusters, matrix, and dendrogram.
stages.reference: After one merge, replace the two old groups by their combined group and update linkage distances. Repeat. A complete n-point agglomerative tree has n−1 merges and ends in one group. A display may stop earlier at a chosen number. The procedure is greedy and does not reconsider previous merges.

stages.title: The Family Tree (Dendrogram)
stages.question: What does dendrogram height represent?
stages.miniPlan: One merge annotated with the selected criterion.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight a branch and its original members; never imply all linkage heights mean the same distance.
stages.reference: Read upwards from the original leaves. Each join names the groups merged and the linkage value then used. Adjacent leaves may be far apart in the original data; their left-right order is a drawing choice. Rotate a branch without changing its merges and the clustering remains the same.

stages.title: Cutting the Tree
stages.question: How does a horizontal cut produce K groups?
stages.miniPlan: Cut height → intersected branches → memberships.
stages.interactionPlan: Drag or numerically set the cut; keep leaf identity and colors stable across nearby cuts.
stages.reference: A horizontal cut determines connected groups below it. Large jumps in height can suggest candidate cuts, but do not prove natural categories. Compare stability and suitable measures such as silhouette, with attention to the distance and task. n−K merges fixes a count even when equal heights make a height-only rule less clear.

stages.title: The Detective's Challenge
stages.question: How sensitive is the tree to preprocessing?
stages.miniPlan: Same data under raw scale, standardized scale, and one outlier.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare alternative trees with stable leaf IDs; make each metric change explicit.
stages.reference: Compare the same original observations under each preparation choice. Investigate unusual points instead of deleting them merely to make tidy clusters. Repeatable groups under several choices are evidence of robustness, not proof of real categories. Explain which model choices caused changes.

stages.title: Synthesis & Recap
stages.question: When is this preferable to K-Means?
stages.miniPlan: Output, K choice, geometry, scale, and computational tradeoffs.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a method for a scenario and justify the tradeoff; include stability and domain validation.
stages.reference: K-means asks for K before fitting and returns one flat partition. Hierarchical clustering returns a merge tree and allows later cuts. Runtime depends on implementation and data size; neither is universally faster or more meaningful. A standard fitted hierarchy does not automatically give a prediction rule for a new point. Report distance, linkage, scaling, cut and stability evidence.

hierarchical-clustering.title: Hierarchical Clustering
hierarchical-clustering.intro: Start with one group per point and merge groups step by step. Read the history as a tree, then choose a cut for a flat grouping.
hierarchical-clustering.prerequisite: Simple distances and reading a two-axis plot.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why can 99% accuracy be useless?
stages.miniPlan: 99 negatives and one positive under an always-negative rule.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the missed positive and its cost before introducing a metric dashboard.
stages.reference: The positive class is the case we choose to flag. Sensitivity is recall, TP/(TP+FN). Specificity is TN/(TN+FP). Accuracy can be dominated by negatives when positives are rare. Define the action and error costs instead of treating 99% as automatically useful.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: Why does prevalence change precision?
stages.miniPlan: Actual positives versus all predicted positives.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep sensitivity/specificity fixed while changing prevalence; separate this from threshold-induced changes.
stages.reference: Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Even a small false-positive rate can generate many false alerts when there are many negatives. Prevalence can change predictive values while sensitivity and specificity stay fixed in a hypothetical comparison. In real new populations, those rates may change too, so verify them rather than assuming only prevalence differs.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How many false alerts occur in the worked example?
