stages.miniPlan: 10,000 → 100 positive / 9,900 negative → TP90 / FP495.
stages.interactionPlan: Correct the counts, 585 alerts, and 15.4% precision; link the full confusion matrix to a workload view.
stages.reference: The complete counts are TP=90, FN=10, FP=495, TN=9,405. Alerts = 90+495=585. Precision = 90/585≈15.4%. The 5% false-positive rate is measured among the 9,900 negatives, not among all alerts or all cases. This is a constructed example illustrating denominators, not a real screening validation.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Which tradeoffs matter for rare positives?
stages.miniPlan: Recall, precision, PR/ROC, calibration, cost, and capacity.
stages.interactionPlan: Explain each with one denominator or decision; replace generic reasoning prose with linked mini examples.
stages.reference: ROC uses recall and false-positive rate. Precision–recall uses recall and the reliability of alerts. Neither curve chooses the operating cutoff for us. Weighting changes the training objective; resampling changes the training examples. Synthetic examples can be unrealistic and must stay inside folds. Probability calibration may need checking after sampling or class-frequency changes.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What happens when we lower the threshold?
stages.miniPlan: Alerts, missed positives, false alerts, and expected cost.
stages.interactionPlan: Use fixed validation score distributions or explicitly label the current scenario model; give a capacity constraint.
stages.reference: Use the same validation scores while changing only the cutoff. Lowering it expands the set of predicted positives. True positives and false positives cannot fall in that fixed comparison, while precision can move either way at individual steps. Convert the counts into review workload and expected cost using explicit assumptions.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: Why can resampling mislead evaluation?
stages.miniPlan: Training-only resampling versus natural evaluation prevalence.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare a falsely balanced test report with natural-prevalence precision; explain recalibration conditions.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Evaluation needs a relevant positive frequency and case mix. The positive labels, costs and capacity assumptions must be credible. Preserve appropriate group or time structure.

When the method fails

Keep evaluation prevalence and case mix relevant to deployment, or use justified weighting and explain it. Oversampling before folds can put closely related or duplicated examples into both training and validation. Resampling must happen within training. Do not report balanced-test precision as if it came from the natural deployment population.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How do we choose a usable operating point?
stages.miniPlan: Costs/capacity → train-fold weighting/resampling → validation threshold.
stages.interactionPlan: Lock a feasible choice before final test; preserve group/time structure as needed.
stages.reference: Define the positive class, actions, costs and any capacity limits. Use a split suited to class balance and related groups or time. Learn weighting, resampling and calibration within development. Choose the cutoff there and evaluate the frozen procedure on a separate final sample.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should accompany the final score?
stages.miniPlan: Prevalence, counts, threshold, PR metrics, calibration, uncertainty.
stages.interactionPlan: Generate a concise decision report with investigation workload, not just a percentage.
stages.reference: What to report: Show the confusion counts, prevalence, threshold, review volume, precision, recall, specificity and any appropriate curve summaries. Explain probability calibration and uncertainty methods. A high ROC-AUC does not guarantee that alerts are affordable or reliable at the chosen cutoff.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I compute workload for a new prevalence?
stages.miniPlan: A fresh cohort with fixed sensitivity and specificity.
stages.interactionPlan: Complete TP/FP and precision; use feedback specific to confusing specificity with precision.
stages.reference: For a new total N, positives are N×prevalence and negatives are the remainder. Apply sensitivity to positives and false-positive rate to negatives. Then add true and false alerts before computing precision. These counts may be expected rather than integer observed counts; label the calculation accordingly.

imbalanced-classification.title: Imbalanced Classification
imbalanced-classification.intro: When positives are rare, count the alerts and misses before trusting a percentage. See why a small false-alarm rate can still create lots of work.
imbalanced-classification.prerequisite: Confusion-matrix counts, percentages, precision and recall.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What is stored by KNN?
stages.miniPlan: One labeled row and its two coordinates.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an observation and explain that training largely stores usable examples rather than a boundary formula.
stages.reference: A label is the known answer for a training row. A query is the new point we want to label. In a simple fruit example, three neighbours labelled Apple, Apple and Orange give two Apple votes and one Orange vote. KNN predicts Apple. It stores examples rather than fitting a coefficient equation. It still relies on useful measurements, distance and representative training coverage.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.question: What makes a feature useful for distance?
stages.miniPlan: Relevant signal versus a seeded irrelevant feature.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare neighbor identity after adding noise; do not choose features from final test outcomes.
stages.reference: A row ID may be just an identifier rather than a useful measurement. But do not declare a field useless from its name alone: dates or collection conditions can matter in some tasks. Choose inputs using the task and validation evidence, not the final test. Extra dimensions can make all distances less informative even after scaling.

stages.title: Keep training, validation and test separate
stages.question: Why separate development and final evaluation?
stages.miniPlan: Immutable train/validation/test membership.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the split and keep held-out labels out of the neighbor pool.
stages.reference: Never let a validation point vote as its own training neighbour. Select features, scaling, K and weights using development data. A final test must stay out of those choices. If observations are related, split whole related groups appropriately. Very small held-out examples illustrate the calculation but do not give stable performance estimates.

stages.title: Feature Scaling
stages.question: Why do units affect neighbors?
stages.miniPlan: Each feature's contribution to distance.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch a training-fitted scaler on the same data; never refit scaling on a queried/test row.
stages.reference: Min-max scaling is (value−training minimum)/(training maximum−training minimum). With value 7, minimum 2 and maximum 9, that is 5/7≈.71. New values may fall outside 0–1; do not secretly refit the scale on them. Scaling is a choice about what near means, not a guarantee of equal feature importance. If units already have a useful shared meaning, automatic rescaling may be unwanted.

stages.title: Measuring Distance
stages.question: How is distance calculated?
stages.miniPlan: Delta x, delta y, squared terms, total.
stages.interactionPlan: Select two points and trace the calculation; offer numeric query coordinates alongside direct manipulation.
stages.reference: For query (.45,.55) and point (.50,.65), the gaps are .05 and .10. Distance = √(.05²+.10²)≈.1118. Squaring means multiply by itself; a square root reverses that operation for a nonnegative value. Manhattan distance adds absolute axis gaps instead. Match the distance to the measurement types and application; scaling cannot rescue irrelevant inputs.

stages.title: Choosing K
stages.question: Why does K change the behavior?
stages.miniPlan: Small-K versus large-K neighbor sets.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub K on fixed data; show a query's changing vote and validation performance.
stages.reference: K is a hyperparameter: a setting chosen by validation rather than a fitted weight. Small K can follow noise; large K can miss local structure. Odd K avoids equal counts for uniform voting between two classes, but does not prevent every type of tie. There is no universally best K for every dataset.

stages.title: Finding Neighbors
stages.question: Which observations are the nearest?
stages.miniPlan: A sorted distance list with row IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight the first K entries and expand the neighborhood; do not move observations to create the animation.
stages.reference: The distance ranking chooses the neighbours; their labels then supply the vote. If distances tie at the K boundary, use a fixed tie rule so rerunning does not silently select different points. Inspect IDs, distances and labels in the receipt rather than inferring the selection only from colours.

stages.title: The Majority Vote
stages.question: How do neighbors vote?
stages.miniPlan: Counts or distance weights, denominator, and tie rule.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal votes one neighbor at a time; distinguish vote fraction from calibrated probability.
stages.reference: A weighted vote can tie even with odd K. Multiclass voting can also tie. Inverse-distance weights cannot divide by zero. This notebook handles exact matches using the labels of those exact matches. A neighbour class fraction is a local estimate; it is not automatically a well-calibrated probability for future cases.

stages.title: Decision Boundary
stages.question: Where do predictions change?
stages.miniPlan: Two nearby query points with different winning votes.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query through a persistent decision surface; recompute surface only when data or K changes.
stages.reference: KNN does not fit one fixed coefficient formula, so it is called nonparametric. That does not mean it has no assumptions. Its boundary comes from the distances and votes. Larger K often smooths local changes, but does not guarantee a straight boundary. Inspect the actual regions and validation errors instead of assuming one shape from K alone.

stages.title: Classify new validation points
stages.question: How do unseen points get a label?
stages.miniPlan: Query → scaling → neighbors → vote.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through a fixed evaluation example without inserting its true label into training.
stages.reference: Use the same feature order, units and fitted scaling for new rows. Search training examples only. Compare the resulting prediction with a known validation label afterward, rather than letting that label enter the vote. Later evaluation data must reflect the kinds of rows the deployed system will receive.

stages.title: Evaluating the Model
stages.question: What does the confusion matrix count?
stages.miniPlan: One case's actual/predicted pair.
stages.interactionPlan: Select errors to locate their queries; use validation for ongoing exploration and reserve final test for a locked run.
stages.reference: Precision asks how often a predicted positive is correct. Recall asks how many actual positives were found. Accuracy can hide a rare class being missed. The notebook's small validation counts are teaching examples. Do not rename them final-test results while choices are still changing.

stages.title: The Effect of K
stages.question: How do we choose K?
stages.miniPlan: Fold-level validation errors with uncertainty across splits.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare a precomputed candidate sweep; avoid repeated final-test optimization.
stages.reference: This lab computes leave-one-out cross-validation on its 48 training rows: hold out one training row, predict from the others, and repeat. Its scaling must also be fitted without the held-out row. In larger tasks, several-fold evaluation may be more practical; choose a split suited to time or related groups. A separate five-fold illustration has scores 75%,88%,92%,90% for K=1,3,5,7. An elbow is only a visual aid, not a replacement for scores and uncertainty. Refit the chosen procedure on all development training data before an untouched final evaluation.
stages.experiment: Compare the training-only leave-one-out scores across K. Move K to a different point and compare its CV score with the separate validation score. Neither uses final-test labels.

stages.title: Strengths and Weaknesses
stages.question: When does KNN become unreliable or expensive?
stages.miniPlan: Density, dimensionality, scaling, missingness, and query cost.
stages.interactionPlan: Add an irrelevant dimension or reduce local density in a labeled toy example.
stages.reference: Many inputs can make distances increasingly alike, called the curse of dimensionality. Common classes can dominate local votes. Brute-force prediction checks every stored point; search structures or approximations can reduce that cost but have their own limits. Validate meaningful coverage, rare-class errors, distance choices and resource use on the intended deployment population.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: Can I explain a new prediction?
stages.miniPlan: A compact neighbor receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Let the learner choose K, query location, and vote rule; capture a before/after comparison and ask why it changed.
stages.reference: Hold the sample fixed while comparing settings. If you also draw a new dataset, several causes of change are mixed together. Explain the new point's location, scaling, selected neighbours, labels, vote and final prediction. That trace is more informative than saying the colour changed.

knn.title: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
knn.intro: To label a new point, find nearby examples with known labels and let them vote. See why the definition of nearby matters.
knn.prerequisite: Reading a two-axis plot, fractions, and simple distances.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What do the labeled clouds represent?
stages.miniPlan: One observation, two features, and a class.
stages.interactionPlan: Link table and point before introducing ellipses or a separating direction.
stages.reference: This is supervised learning: the training rows already have labels. The plotted clouds are small teaching datasets, not a claim that real fruit or other classes always have these shapes. An input is also called a feature. The class is the answer we want to predict.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.question: Why does feature choice matter?
stages.miniPlan: Two informative features versus a redundant or noisy one.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a seeded feature alternative using validation; retain feature units and provenance.
stages.reference: Measurements with little relevant information can make fitting harder. Redundant or nearly identical features can make covariance difficult to invert. Prepare features within training data. Check validation results rather than choosing inputs by which final-test score looks best.

stages.title: Keep training, validation and test separate
stages.question: Which data estimate the class distributions?
stages.miniPlan: Split roles and class counts.
stages.interactionPlan: Show training observations contributing to estimates; keep held-out rows visually distinct.
stages.reference: Training estimates the means, covariance and any data-derived priors. Validation is for development comparisons. An untouched test is for the finished procedure. The live example exposes validation results during exploration; do not treat every changing display as a new final-test evaluation.

stages.title: Group by Class
stages.question: Why group observations by class?
stages.miniPlan: Labeled rows sorted into class-specific columns.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush one class and reveal its sample size without changing point positions.
stages.reference: A multivariate Gaussian is a bell-shaped probability model in several inputs. Its contour is an equal-density outline, not a hard wall containing all points. LDA assumes the class covariance matrices are equal. Real data may differ from this model, so inspect predictions and calibration rather than treating the assumptions as verified by a tidy plot.

stages.title: Compute Class Means
stages.question: What is a class mean?
stages.miniPlan: Coordinate-wise average of three points.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw deviations into a class center; show the center can sit where no observation exists.
stages.reference: For a class with two inputs, μ contains the average of input 1 and the average of input 2. The symbol μ means mean. Class labels are used to form these separate averages. A new query point is not added to the class centre before it is classified.

stages.title: Within-Class Scatter
stages.question: What does within-class scatter describe?
stages.miniPlan: Two variances and one covariance.
stages.interactionPlan: Link covariance-matrix entries to ellipse spread and tilt with a short symbol dictionary.
stages.reference: Covariance is a table of spread measurements. Positive covariance means the two inputs tend to rise together within a class; negative means one tends to fall as the other rises. Near-zero covariance means little linear co-movement, not no relationship of any kind. The diagonal gives variances, or average squared spread, rather than standard deviations.

stages.title: The Shared Covariance Assumption
stages.question: Why share one covariance estimate?
stages.miniPlan: Separate class covariances versus pooled covariance.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare shared and separate shapes; explain the stability-versus-flexibility tradeoff.
stages.reference: Pooling combines within-class covariance estimates with weights based on their available degrees of freedom. It does not just calculate the total cloud's covariance around one grand centre. After moving both fitted centres to zero, LDA's two fitted outlines have the same shape. Observed class clouds may still have different raw shapes.

stages.title: Between-Class Scatter
stages.question: What counts as between-class separation?
stages.miniPlan: Class means versus the overall mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight mean differences independently from within-class spread.
stages.reference: Within-class scatter describes spread around each class centre. Between-class scatter describes separation between centres. LDA compares these after projection. The ratio J(w)=wᵀS_Bw/(wᵀS_Ww) rewards separation relative to within-class spread. This is not simply the direction with the largest overall data spread, as in PCA.

stages.title: The Optimal Direction
stages.question: Why project along this direction?
stages.miniPlan: Separation divided by projected within-class spread.
stages.interactionPlan: Rotate a candidate projection, then reveal the fitted LDA direction; distinguish this from PCA.
stages.reference: For two classes, w is proportional to S_W⁻¹(μ₁−μ₂), when the needed inverse exists. The inverse adjusts for spread and tilt. A projected score is a weighted combination of the original inputs. It is not a third original measurement or automatically a probability. LDA projection can give at most K−1 separating dimensions for K classes.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.question: Why is the boundary linear?
stages.miniPlan: Shared quadratic terms that cancel in a score difference.
stages.interactionPlan: Link mean, covariance, and prior changes to the boundary; keep algebra in expandable steps.
stages.reference: The prior π_k is how common class k is before seeing this row's inputs. It may come from training proportions or an explicit choice appropriate to the task. LDA's score is xᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k − ½μ_kᵀΣ⁻¹μ_k + log(π_k). The common quadratic part cancels when comparing scores. The largest score wins. In a separate illustration, scores 2.31 and −1.44 choose the first class.

stages.title: Classify new validation points
stages.question: How is a new case classified?
stages.miniPlan: Class score terms and the chosen class.
stages.interactionPlan: Move/select a query and compare its class scores; probability claims must use the model assumptions.
stages.reference: The decision depends on centre distance measured relative to the shared shape and on the prior. A point far along a broad direction may be less unusual than the same raw distance along a narrow direction. The predicted label and model probability still need validation against the intended application and error costs.

stages.title: Evaluating the Model
stages.question: How do we judge the classifier?
stages.miniPlan: Confusion counts, chosen positive class, metric denominators.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush validation mistakes; use a separate locked final-test demonstration.
stages.reference: Name which class is positive before reading TP, FP, TN and FN. A false positive predicts the positive class for an actual negative. A false negative misses an actual positive. These classification errors are not automatically the Type I and Type II errors of a hypothesis test. Tiny teaching samples cannot establish stable production accuracy.

stages.title: Reading LDA Output
stages.question: What does an LDA summary mean?
stages.miniPlan: Priors, means, shared covariance, coefficients.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an output item and highlight the quantity it controls; clarify empirical versus specified priors.
stages.reference: The covariance table explains spread and tilt; means locate centres; priors supply baseline class frequencies. Coefficients combine these fitted summaries into a boundary. Report input units, sample split, preprocessing, priors, assumptions and task-relevant validation scores. A perfect score on easy simulated data does not guarantee performance on later real data.

stages.title: Assumptions & Limitations
stages.question: When is the shared-shape assumption costly?
stages.miniPlan: Similar shapes / unequal shapes / small samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fixed LDA and QDA scenarios on identical splits; discuss singularity and regularization.
stages.reference: LDA can struggle with misspecified class shapes, influential unusual points, highly redundant inputs or too little data for covariance estimation. An absence of outliers is not a formal requirement for computing the classifier. Shrinkage can stabilize covariance. QDA, logistic regression or other classifiers answer related prediction tasks with different assumptions; choose using comparable validation rather than a universal ranking.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: Can I predict how the boundary will move?
stages.miniPlan: Before/after settings and class-score receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one mean, spread, or prior; preserve dataset seed and ask the learner to explain the outcome.
stages.reference: Hold everything else fixed and change one centre, prior or covariance setting. Trace the same point's two scores and resulting label. Distinguish a changed dataset from a changed assumption in fitting. Neither experiment demonstrates a causal feature effect.

lda.title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
lda.intro: Describe each labelled group with a centre and a shared spread shape. Use those fitted summaries to classify a new point.
lda.prerequisite: Averages, two-axis plots, and the meaning of training and validation.

stages.title: It Starts with Data
stages.question: What is the binary outcome?
stages.miniPlan: One weather/day row and whether a purchase occurred.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the row to the plotted observation; label class and feature units independently.
stages.reference: In a separate shop example, inputs include temperature and sunny weather; the label records whether someone bought ice cream. Here 1 means the designated positive class, not one unit purchased. Probability 0.5 means 50%; 0 means impossible and 1 certain within a probability model. The notebook uses small simulated examples, not a verified sales model.
stages.experiment: Move the new point using Query x and Query z. Then move the decision threshold: blue predicts 0 and red predicts 1. The dots keep their known labels, and the fitted probabilities do not change.

stages.title: Why Lines Break
stages.question: Why is an ordinary line awkward for probability?
stages.miniPlan: A linear prediction below zero or above one.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare the raw linear score and a probability output using the same observations.
stages.reference: The raw score adds up weighted inputs and an intercept. The sigmoid turns that score into a valid probability. A finite score gives a value strictly between 0 and 1. That bound alone does not prove the estimated probability is accurate.
stages.experiment: Compare the thin red line with the green sigmoid. Move the decision threshold and watch the blue/red probability field slide. The cutoff changes labels; it does not move the curves.

stages.title: From a Raw Score to a Probability
stages.question: What does the sigmoid do?
stages.miniPlan: z → exp(−z) → probability, with a small value table.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub z and move a marker along the sigmoid; keep this distinct from changing a fitted coefficient.
stages.reference: s = intercept + weight₁×input₁ + weight₂×input₂ + … . Then p = 1/(1+e^(−s)). e is a fixed mathematical number used by the exponential function. s is this model's raw score, not a standardized z-score. The model calculates it separately for each row. A teaching slider may inspect that conversion, but training learns weights rather than one free score for every row.
stages.experiment: Move the input coordinates and follow the gold point along the S-curve. Then move the decision threshold. Watch the two-colour field change while the fitted curve and probability stay fixed.

stages.title: Weighted Clues
stages.question: How do weighted clues form s?
stages.miniPlan: Intercept plus each feature's signed contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one input or coefficient at a time; synchronize the contribution receipt and score-to-probability diagram.
stages.reference: A weight is also called a coefficient. Each input-times-weight product adds to the raw score. Learn any input scaling from training data. Scaling can help training and make weight penalties more comparable. Large input units do not automatically dominate a fitted linear model because its coefficients account for units. This lab learns weights from training rows; the input controls explore the saved prediction rule.
stages.experiment: Change x, then z, and follow their weighted contributions into the probability. In the map below, move the decision threshold: the blue/red regions move while the weights and probability stay fixed.

stages.title: Learning from Mistakes
stages.question: What does learning minimize?
stages.miniPlan: One prediction's log loss and gradient direction.
stages.interactionPlan: Step an actual parameter update and plot loss; distinguish gradients from the optimizer's action.
stages.reference: Binary log loss is −[y log(p)+(1−y)log(1−p)]. If the true class is 1, probabilities .95, .55 and .05 give losses about .05, .60 and 3.00. These are one-row examples; training usually averages over rows. A regularization penalty can discourage large weights. Gradient descent takes small downhill steps; its learning rate is the step size. Other optimizers can fit logistic regression too. Excessively large steps may fail to settle.
stages.experiment: Set the true-class probability to 0.9, then 0.1. Predict which penalty is larger. The point and receipt calculate this one-case loss; they do not retrain the classifier.

stages.title: Drawing the Line
stages.question: Why does a probability need a decision threshold?
stages.miniPlan: Probability / threshold / resulting action.
stages.interactionPlan: Move the threshold and immediately update labels on development data; preserve continuous probabilities.
stages.reference: For probability .62, a .50 threshold predicts 1 and a .70 threshold predicts 0. Lower thresholds catch at least as many positives and usually add false alarms on fixed data. Raising a threshold does not guarantee that precision rises at every step. Select it using validation data, error costs, class frequency and capacity. Keep the final test out of that choice.

stages.title: Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data
stages.question: Which mistakes does this threshold create?
stages.miniPlan: Confusion-cell definitions with their actual denominators.
stages.interactionPlan: Select TP/FP/FN/TN to brush corresponding validation cases; update counts and costs together.
stages.reference: TP means predicted 1 and actual 1. TN means predicted 0 and actual 0. FP is predicted 1 but actual 0. FN is predicted 0 but actual 1. Accuracy uses all rows; precision uses predicted positives; recall uses actual positives. F1 combines precision and recall and can be undefined under some zero-denominator conventions. The final-test snapshot remains separate from ongoing validation changes.

stages.title: The Validation ROC Curve
stages.question: What does the ROC curve summarize?
stages.miniPlan: TPR and FPR denominator mini diagrams.
stages.interactionPlan: Sweep a validation threshold and move its ROC operating point; keep AUC separate from accuracy and calibration.
stages.reference: ROC plots recall, TP/(TP+FN), against false-positive rate, FP/(FP+TN). AUC is the area under that curve. It summarizes positive-versus-negative ranking; ties count half. AUC .5 is the random-ranking benchmark, but some useful non-random rankings can also have AUC .5. AUC is not accuracy, calibration or a threshold recommendation. Small validation sets give coarse steps and uncertain estimates.

stages.title: What the Numbers Mean
stages.question: What is an odds ratio?
stages.miniPlan: Probability ↔ odds ↔ log-odds with one coefficient example.
stages.interactionPlan: Change a feature by one unit while holding others fixed; avoid interpreting coefficient size as causal importance.
stages.reference: At p=.75, odds are .75/.25=3, or 3 to 1. The raw score s is the natural logarithm of the odds. Adding a weight to that score multiplies the odds by e^weight. This gives the odds ratio: OR=e^weight. OR=2 doubles the odds, not the probability and not the odds ratio itself. Interpretation holds other modeled inputs fixed. For standardized inputs, one unit means one unit on that transformed scale. These associations do not prove that changing an input causes the outcome.
stages.experiment: Read each input weight and its e^weight odds multiplier. Change the data pattern or weight penalty and compare the saved multipliers. A one-unit input change holds the other input fixed.

stages.title: The Full Picture
stages.question: What is locked before the final test?
stages.miniPlan: Training, validation choices, locked model, final evaluation.
stages.interactionPlan: Preserve the existing one-time reveal; demonstrate that threshold changes cannot silently tune the sealed test.
stages.reference: Fit input preparation and weights on training data. Compare settings and cutoffs on validation data. Lock the whole procedure, then report the final-test results with sample sizes, error costs, suitable metrics and uncertainty. Repeatedly optimizing against the test makes it part of development. A fresh independent test is then needed for a new final claim.

logistic-regression.title: Logistic Regression
logistic-regression.intro: Turn clues into a probability, then turn that probability into a yes/no decision. Keep these two steps separate.
logistic-regression.prerequisite: Fractions, percentages, and multiplying then adding numbers.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: What might an empty cell mean?
stages.miniPlan: Missing, structural absence, and a real zero.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a missing value and show possible mechanisms without pretending the mechanism is identifiable from appearance.
stages.reference: A data dictionary records what each column and special marker means. A blank might mean a sensor failed or a question did not apply. Zero might be a real value. Keep those meanings distinct. A convenient replacement can change the question or create a false numeric order.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What assumptions do filling and encoding add?
stages.miniPlan: Imputation assumptions and unordered/ordered category geometry.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare a raw row with transformed columns; name the modeling goal before choosing a method.
stages.reference: Some encodings have learned statistics; others use a fixed declared mapping. Save which is which. Fit any data-learned fill, category set or frequency within training. Preserve raw columns so the transformation can be inspected and alternatives compared.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: Why can mean filling distort an analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Observed values, filled value, and changed variability.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a high-income missingness example; preserve the uncertainty about unseen values.
stages.reference: If high earners are more likely to leave income blank, filling with the observed mean pulls those rows towards the middle. It can distort means and spread. A missingness indicator records whether the value was absent; it may help prediction, but does not prove a missing-at-random assumption for statistical inference.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do MCAR, MAR, MNAR, and encoding differ?
stages.miniPlan: Mechanism assumptions separately from representation choices.
stages.interactionPlan: Use one miniature for mechanisms and one for one-hot/ordinal/target encoding; do not overload a single chart.
stages.reference: MCAR means missingness does not depend on the relevant observed or missing values. MAR means, after conditioning on observed information, it does not depend on the missing value. MNAR means dependence on the unobserved value remains. These are assumptions, not diagnoses proved by a chart. One-hot makes separate yes/no columns for unordered categories. Ordinal encoding asserts an order, so use it only when that order is justified.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: How should methods be compared fairly?
stages.miniPlan: Scenario assumptions, missing rate, method, target metric.
stages.interactionPlan: Replace fixed universal bias rankings with computed toy scenarios or clearly labeled illustrative indices; expose sensitivity to the mechanism.
stages.reference: The best choice depends on why values are missing, the variables and whether the goal is prediction or estimation. Compare under plausible scenarios, including uncertainty and data quality. The live examples illustrate those scenarios; they are not a universal ranking of imputers.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can imputation not recover automatically?
stages.miniPlan: Uncertainty, unseen categories, leakage, and false ordering.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a target-encoding leakage case and a category-order counterexample.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

The analysis relies on stated assumptions about why values are missing. Category representation must match meaningful order or lack of order. Learn data-based transforms only within training.

When the method fails

Single imputation treats one filled value as if known, often understating inference uncertainty. Multiple imputation combines several plausible filled datasets, accounting for within- and between-imputation variation under its assumptions. Target encoding summarizes outcomes by category and needs fold-safe or cross-fitted training representations. Plain numeric category codes can create unjustified distances.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: What belongs in the fitted pipeline?
stages.miniPlan: Split → train-fit imputer/encoder → frozen transform.
stages.interactionPlan: Step a new category through the saved unknown-level policy; show cross-fitting for target encoding.
stages.reference: Profile blanks and category levels, distinguish structural absence from accidental missingness, split appropriately, and learn transforms inside training. Save category reference levels and unknown-level behavior. Frequency and target encoders need suitable fitting boundaries. New categories should follow the saved policy rather than cause an unexplained failure or arbitrary numeric label.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What must be documented?
stages.miniPlan: Missingness rate, assumptions, method, references, unknown policy, sensitivity.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a transformation record from the current scenario without implying assumptions were proven.
stages.reference: What to report: State rates by column, missingness assumptions, imputation models, number of imputations where relevant, category meanings, reference levels and unknown-category handling. Separate facts observed in the data from assumptions about unobserved values. Report sensitivity to reasonable alternatives.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I choose a safe transformation?
stages.miniPlan: A new unordered category or missing-not-at-random case.
stages.interactionPlan: Ask for the assumption and pipeline placement, not merely a method name; retain all answer explanations.
stages.reference: Check why the values are absent, what numerical geometry the encoding creates, and which rows learned the rule. A method can be appropriate for prediction yet unsuitable for an inferential target. Keep uncertainty and deployment input rules explicit.

missing-data-encoding.title: Missing Data & Encoding
missing-data-encoding.intro: An empty cell needs an explanation. Choose clear ways to fill missing values and represent categories without inventing information or leaking answers.
missing-data-encoding.prerequisite: Reading tables and the roles of training and validation.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.question: Why can extra flexibility hurt new predictions?
stages.miniPlan: Training and validation errors on the same candidate models.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a seeded noise feature; avoid claiming more features always cause overfitting.
stages.reference: Overfitting means sample-specific patterns hurt predictions outside training. More parameters do not automatically cause it, and fewer do not guarantee success. A model-selection plan compares useful predictive loss and practical costs under a suitable evaluation design.

stages.title: The n-p Puzzle
stages.question: What if several coefficient choices give the same fit?
stages.miniPlan: n, p, rank, and two equally fitting coefficient vectors.
stages.interactionPlan: Show nonunique coefficients separately from generalization; introduce regularization as an additional constraint.
stages.reference: A design matrix is the table of model input columns. If its columns are not independent, several coefficient vectors may fit equally well. This is identifiability, a different issue from interpolation or overfitting. Ridge, Lasso or other constraints can support prediction, but they do not prove which overlapping variable has a causal effect.

stages.title: Picking the Best Team
stages.question: Why not search every subset?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate counts for small p, then 2^p.
stages.interactionPlan: Step forward/backward selection on a tiny example; describe computational growth without saying all sizes are impossible.
stages.reference: Forward selection adds an input at a time. Backward selection removes one at a time. Stepwise or hybrid procedures do both under stated rules. These shortcuts do not guarantee the best of all subsets. Feature selection belongs inside validation folds, so the held-out rows do not influence the chosen subset.
stages.experiment: Change polynomial degree to change the number of optional columns. Count the include/leave-out combinations. These dots show candidates, not a fitted exhaustive-search result.

stages.title: The Scorecards
stages.question: What does each scorecard penalize?
stages.miniPlan: Criterion / objective / direction / assumptions / parameter count.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare identical fitted candidates; standardize AIC/BIC/Cp conventions and distinguish ranking-equivalent rescalings.
stages.reference: Under comparable likelihood models, AIC = −2 log likelihood + 2k and BIC = −2 log likelihood + k log n, with k fitted parameters and n observations. Shared constants or per-row scaling can produce equivalent score presentations. Lower is better within the relevant comparison. Adjusted R² uses a different scale, with higher better. Mallows' Cp has its own variance estimate and conventions. Name the criterion and parameter count; none automatically guarantees new-data performance.
stages.experiment: Change degree and compare the fit term, AIC penalty and BIC penalty. Add each penalty to the same fit term by hand before checking the totals.

stages.title: The Shrinking Trick
stages.question: What does shrinkage trade away?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction error plus coefficient penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Change lambda on a fixed standardized training matrix; keep the intercept treatment explicit.
stages.reference: The fitting objective combines error with a penalty. λ=0 removes that penalty; larger λ usually increases its influence. Penalizing coefficients depends on feature units, so choose scaling deliberately and fit it only within training folds. A smaller coefficient is not automatically an unimportant or causally irrelevant input.

stages.title: Ridge Regression (L2)
stages.question: Why does Ridge usually keep all predictors?
stages.miniPlan: Two correlated coefficients and the L2 penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Animate actual solution paths; replace the absolute never-zero claim and explain units.
stages.reference: This lab's Ridge objective is MSE/2 + λΣβ_j²/2, with the intercept excluded. The sum Σ adds over non-intercept coefficients. Ridge generally does not select a sparse list, although special coefficients can still equal zero. Its stabilizing effect does not guarantee that every penalty value improves validation error.
stages.experiment: Increase lambda in this Ridge section. Watch squared-weight shrinkage and the validation score. At lambda zero, no coefficient penalty is applied.

stages.title: Lasso Regression (L1)
stages.question: Why can Lasso produce zeros?
stages.miniPlan: L1 constraint geometry and a coefficient path.
stages.interactionPlan: Follow a coefficient to zero; show instability under correlated features and an Elastic Net comparison in deeper reading.
stages.reference: Lasso uses an L1 penalty, a sum of absolute coefficient sizes. Its shape has a corner at zero, which can produce exact zeros. This is selection by the fitting rule, not proof that omitted variables have no effect. Check selection across resamples. Elastic Net combines L1 and squared L2 penalties and may behave differently when inputs overlap.
stages.experiment: Increase lambda in this Lasso section. Watch whether coefficients reach zero, and compare the validation error. Do not assume a zero coefficient proves a useless or noncausal input.

stages.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
stages.question: How do we choose lambda honestly?
stages.miniPlan: Fold-safe transforms and a validation-error curve.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidates using the same folds; expose the one-SE choice only with an explicit uncertainty calculation.
stages.reference: Use folds suited to the structure: whole related groups together, forward-time splits for forecasting, or suitable class-stratified splits where needed. Refit imputation, scaling, encoding, selection and compression inside each training fold. Nested validation uses an inner loop to select and an outer loop to assess the whole selection process. It reduces selection bias under a suitable design; it does not guarantee a perfectly unbiased estimate in every setting.

stages.title: The "Super-Variable" Secret
stages.question: How do PCR and PLS differ?
stages.miniPlan: Whether y participates in choosing the new directions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare a high-variance irrelevant direction with a predictive direction; fit all transforms inside training folds.
stages.reference: PCR means principal component regression. It uses directions of input variation, which may not be the directions useful for predicting y. PLS means partial least squares; it uses input–outcome relationships to construct directions. The number of components is another development choice. Neither method is automatically a causal explanation or a guarantee that useful information is preserved.
stages.experiment: Change the data pattern or noise. Compare the blue PCA direction with the gold first-PLS direction from the same two centred input columns. This illustrates directions, not full PCR/PLS prediction performance.

stages.title: Decision Helper
stages.question: Which tradeoff matters for this task?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction, compact explanation, correlated inputs, and causal questions.
stages.interactionPlan: Return conditional options with reasons; stop equating feature selection with causal explanation.
stages.reference: Compare latency, memory, interpretability and errors relevant to the application. Sparse weights do not prove a simpler causal story. A model retaining many correlated inputs can still be useful if validated. State the tradeoff and a tie rule for practically similar scores instead of assigning a universal winner.

stages.title: Common Mistakes
stages.question: How does repeated evaluation bias our choices?
stages.miniPlan: Training, repeated validation decisions, sealed test.
stages.interactionPlan: Demonstrate selection optimism and nested evaluation; avoid universal claims about every training score.
stages.reference: Choosing settings after viewing scores is still learning from those rows, even without fitting coefficients on them. Many comparisons can overfit development evidence. A final untouched test or an appropriate outer evaluation checks the selected procedure. Report what was searched, the design and uncertainty rather than hiding the number of attempts.

stages.title: Final Synthesis
stages.question: Can I justify the selected model?
stages.miniPlan: Chosen method, validation basis, preprocessing, limits.
stages.interactionPlan: Produce a short model card from explicit choices; check that no final-test result influenced the selection.
stages.reference: Lock the chosen procedure before final evaluation. State the target, data collection, input timing, transformations, candidates, selection metric and evaluation split. Explain why the choice meets the task and which assumptions remain. New populations or changed conditions may require new evidence.

model-selection.title: Model Selection & Regularization
model-selection.intro: Choose a whole prediction procedure, not just the most impressive training fit. Compare flexibility, stability and new-data errors.
model-selection.prerequisite: Linear and polynomial regression, training/validation splits, and prediction errors.

stages.title: The Multi-Variable World
stages.question: Why use more than one predictor?
stages.miniPlan: Study, sleep, practice, and target in a single student row.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the row to a 2D/3D teaching slice; explicitly name the dimension held fixed.
stages.reference: With two inputs and one outcome, the prediction can be drawn as a plane in three dimensions. One dot is one observed row; its height is the outcome. The vertical gap to the plane is actual minus predicted. More inputs require more dimensions, so a drawing must clearly state which ones are held fixed. The live lab uses two inputs, with the same rows shown across its views.

stages.title: The Secret Recipe
stages.question: How does the equation combine clues?
stages.miniPlan: Term / value / units / contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight one coefficient and its contribution; translate beta and epsilon before matrix notation.
stages.reference: ŷ = b₀+b₁x₁+b₂x₂. ŷ means prediction, b₀ is the intercept, and b₁,b₂ are coefficients. Each coefficient has outcome units per input unit. The fitted plane describes the predicted mean; individual outcomes can differ. An intercept at impossible or unobserved zero inputs may have little practical meaning.

stages.title: Finding the Fit
stages.question: What changes when I adjust one coefficient?
stages.miniPlan: A fixed student's old and new prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Update the plane slice and full-model residual together; keep practice's contribution visible outside the slice.
stages.reference: Use the same observed rows while comparing trial coefficients. The residuals are vertical outcome gaps at each row's own input values. A fixed-input slice can help explain one slope, but it must not silently replace the full prediction used in a residual calculation. The numerical receipt and visual use the same fitted inputs.

stages.title: The Least Squares Method
stages.question: How does least squares select the weights?
stages.miniPlan: A tiny design matrix and residual sum.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal fitted coefficients with one action; retain rank-deficiency and nonunique-solution caveats in deeper detail.
stages.reference: Squaring stops +4 and −4 cancelling: both contribute 16. Least squares minimizes their total across training rows. A design matrix is the table of model input columns, including the intercept. Exact column redundancy gives non-unique ordinary coefficients. A penalty can stabilize a fit, but changes the fitting rule and does not prove causal effects.

stages.title: The Superpower: Holding Constant
stages.question: What does holding constant mean?
stages.miniPlan: Two hypothetical rows differing only in study hours.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide along a fixed-sleep/practice slice; distinguish conditional association from a causal intervention.
stages.reference: If b₁=3, increasing x₁ by one raises the predicted mean by 3 outcome units while x₂ stays fixed. That is an adjusted model association, not a guaranteed gain for one person. Holding a variable fixed may be impossible as a real intervention. Causal interpretation needs a suitable design and assumptions beyond the regression equation.

stages.title: Building the Prediction
stages.question: How is a prediction assembled?
stages.miniPlan: Intercept plus three signed contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a waterfall with a consistent scale and numeric receipt; preserve negative contributions.
stages.reference: For example, intercept 10 plus contributions 6 and −2 gives prediction 14. The sign belongs to the product, so a negative input and negative coefficient make a positive contribution. Check the actual values shown rather than assuming every coefficient is a positive boost.

stages.title: The Spurious Trap
stages.question: Why can an apparent relationship disappear?
stages.miniPlan: Simple versus adjusted coefficient, with a confounder sketch.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fits on the same data; explain why adjustment alone does not establish causality.
stages.reference: A shared cause can create an unadjusted link. Hot weather, for example, may influence both ice-cream sales and beach activity. Adding a relevant predictor can change another coefficient, but does not guarantee all confounding has been removed. A coefficient near zero means little adjusted linear association in this particular fit; it does not prove no real-world effect. Coefficient sizes also depend on units.

stages.title: The Adjusted R² Penalty
stages.question: Why can training R-squared reward useless variables?
stages.miniPlan: Training R², adjusted R², and validation error.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a seeded noise predictor; recompute all three without implying adjusted R² always rejects it.
stages.reference: For an ordinary least-squares model with an intercept, training R²=1−SSE/TSS. Adjusted R²=1−[(1−R²)(n−1)/(n−p−1)], with p predictors and a positive residual degrees-of-freedom denominator. Adjusted R² can rise or fall after adding a predictor. Neither score is an automatic feature-retention rule. Compare held-out prediction error and the purpose of the model too.

stages.title: Reading the Model Output
stages.question: How do I read a regression summary?
stages.miniPlan: Estimate / SE / interval / test statistic / units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a coefficient row and link its interval and prediction effect; replace universal t≈2 shortcuts with conditions.
stages.reference: A coefficient's SE estimates its uncertainty under the model and design assumptions. t is estimate/SE for a zero-coefficient test; a universal cutoff of 2 is not always appropriate. Check residual shape, changing spread, dependence and influence. VIF measures overlap with other predictors. Distinguish an interval for a mean response from a wider interval for a new observation. State categorical reference levels, interactions, evaluation design and limits.

multiple-linear-regression.title: Multiple Linear Regression
multiple-linear-regression.intro: Combine several input clues to predict one number. Follow each contribution and see what holding the other inputs fixed means.
multiple-linear-regression.prerequisite: Simple Linear Regression, averages, and multiplying then adding numbers.

stages.title: The whole idea: learn patterns from examples
stages.question: What does learning from examples mean?
stages.miniPlan: Conventional rule versus learned parameters.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a labeled student example to a prediction; keep the running example consistent with the visuals.
stages.reference: The computed lab is a 2→3→1 binary network: two inputs, three hidden units and one output. Follow those same dimensions through each calculation. The generated data is small and fully inspectable. A network is arithmetic learned from examples, not a literal human brain or a guarantee of understanding.

stages.title: Data becomes features and labels
stages.question: How do rows become inputs and targets?
stages.miniPlan: Raw row, encoded feature vector, separate label.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a student and follow every value; explain dimensions and units before introducing tensors.
stages.reference: A feature is an input clue; a label is the known target. Here the plot shows two numeric inputs and a binary class. A gold query is a point being inspected, not automatically a new training row. Its true label may be used to inspect loss, but must not enter the forward prediction.

stages.title: Clean, encode, scale, then split
stages.question: When should preprocessing be learned?
stages.miniPlan: Split first → fit transforms on train → apply unchanged.
stages.interactionPlan: Correct the heading; contrast a safe pipeline with one that uses held-out statistics.
stages.reference: Check raw errors and the data's meaning. Learned imputation, scaling and encoding belong within training. Validation compares choices and stopping. Final test remains separate. The lab has 48 training rows, 16 validation rows and 16 sealed test rows. Split percentages are examples; independence, timing and intended use decide the appropriate design.

stages.title: A network is layers of tiny calculators
stages.question: What does a layer compute?
stages.miniPlan: Input vector → neuron calculations → output vector.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal one layer at a time without moving all nodes or shrinking annotations.
stages.reference: For neuron j, z_j=w₁j x₁+w₂j x₂+b_j. z is the weighted sum and b the bias. Activation transforms z into the neuron's output. The responses are numerical features; they are not guaranteed to represent human-named ideas such as sleep or effort. More units can add capacity, computation and overfitting risk.

stages.title: One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron
stages.question: Why does each connection have its own weight?
stages.miniPlan: One input feeding two neurons through different weights.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an edge and trace its contribution; changing one weight must not change unrelated edges.
stages.reference: There is no one universal weight for an input. It can connect to several neurons with different multipliers. A negative weight can lower a sum for a positive input. A negative input times a negative weight raises it. Follow the actual products and totals. A weight alone rarely gives a complete human explanation of a distributed network.

stages.title: Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends
stages.question: Why are nonlinear activations necessary?
stages.miniPlan: Two linear layers collapsed into one versus a nonlinear bend.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle activation on a tiny deterministic network; state that extra linear layers alone remain linear.
stages.reference: ReLU(z)=max(0,z): it passes positive values and sets negative ones to zero. Tanh bends into a range from −1 to 1. Sigmoid maps a raw output to a 0–1 probability for a binary task. Softmax converts several class scores into probabilities summing to 1. A regression output can remain an unrestricted number. ReLU does not mean the entire network discards every kind of negative evidence; other units can represent it.

stages.title: Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction
stages.question: What happens in one forward pass?
stages.miniPlan: Multiply → sum → bias → activation receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Step a single student's actual values through the network; preserve the same selected row throughout.
stages.reference: Follow the same gold input through all three hidden response maps. Multiply those responses by output weights, add output bias, then apply sigmoid. A probability .82 leaves .18 for the other binary class under this model. A separate decision threshold turns that probability into a label. No parameter changes during the forward pass.

stages.title: Loss measures how wrong the prediction was
stages.question: What does loss measure?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction, label, selected loss, numeric contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Change the prediction and show the loss curve; explain the difference between a probability, decision, and loss.
stages.reference: For binary targets, loss is −[y log(p)+(1−y)log(1−p)]. If y=1, assigning tiny p produces a large penalty. The training objective averages appropriate row losses, possibly adding a penalty. Loss measures a chosen objective; it is not automatically a measure of practical harm, calibration or fairness.

stages.title: Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients
stages.question: What does backpropagation compute?
stages.miniPlan: Local derivative × upstream derivative.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace gradients backward while keeping weights fixed; make this distinction explicit in the controls.
stages.reference: A gradient is a collection of local slopes. The chain rule connects how one operation changes the next, all the way to loss. Backpropagation computes those slopes using the same parameter snapshot. The gradient points locally uphill; a downhill step goes in the opposite direction. The visible landscape is a two-weight slice with other parameters fixed, not the full high-dimensional surface.

stages.title: The optimizer takes iterative, local steps
stages.question: What does the optimizer change?
stages.miniPlan: Current weight − learning rate × gradient.
stages.interactionPlan: Apply one update; compare step sizes and overshoot in the model behavior without decorative numeric overshoot.
stages.reference: New weight = old weight − rate×gradient. If the gradient is +2 and the rate .1, subtract .2. This is a local step, not proof it reaches the global best fit. Large steps may overshoot. The lab's two-weight step and full-network training updates are separate operations with their scope stated. Rewind restores the previous saved parameters.

stages.title: One update has a strict causal order
stages.question: Why must operations happen in this order?
stages.miniPlan: Forward → loss → gradients → update.
stages.interactionPlan: Require the learner to choose the next operation; snapshot all values for reversible inspection.
stages.reference: A batch is the examples used for one update. An iteration is one update; an epoch is one full pass through the training data. For 1,000 rows and batch size 100, a simple full-pass setup uses 10 iterations per epoch. The lab's ordered cycle makes calculation and update distinct, rather than animating weights during gradient computation.

stages.title: Choose the model before validation gets worse
stages.question: Why monitor validation during training?
stages.miniPlan: Train and validation curves with checkpoint markers.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub real or honestly labeled illustrative epochs; select the best validation checkpoint and preserve test isolation.
stages.reference: Training loss can fall while validation loss worsens, which is evidence to investigate possible overfitting rather than proof of a cause. Choose checkpoints using development rules and uncertainty. Validation choice itself can overfit if tried repeatedly. Compare the two measured curves before changing the training settings.

stages.title: Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters
stages.question: Which settings do humans choose?
stages.miniPlan: Parameter versus hyperparameter table.
stages.interactionPlan: Change layer width, activation, or learning rate in separate experiments; show computation and capacity tradeoffs.
stages.reference: Parameters are learned weights and biases. Hyperparameters describe how the system is built and trained. Changing an activation in this lab restarts the run; changing rate affects later updates. Use validation rather than test feedback for those choices. A simpler model can be preferable if it meets the same need with less cost or uncertainty.

stages.title: Validation checks scores and decisions
stages.question: What is evaluated on the final test set?
stages.miniPlan: Scores, chosen decision threshold, and confusion counts.
stages.interactionPlan: Lock the threshold before reveal; offer a distinct validation workspace for experimentation.
stages.reference: Choose any threshold using development data, then freeze it with all preparation and weights. A .50 model threshold is not an exam's passing mark; it is a cutoff on the model probability. The live confusion matrix uses validation, not exposed final-test labels. A later independent final evaluation concerns the complete selected procedure.

stages.title: Error analysis starts with individual students
stages.question: What can an individual error teach us?
stages.miniPlan: One wrong student's inputs, score, action, true outcome.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush error groups and inspect cases; avoid selecting future model changes by repeated final-test checking.
stages.reference: False positives predict class 1 for actual class 0; false negatives miss actual class 1. Follow mistakes in the input plot and confusion matrix. A threshold change only changes the decision rule, not the fitted probabilities. Check patterns by relevant groups with enough data; one error or one subgroup average can be uncertain.

stages.title: Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle
stages.question: What must be saved with the weights?
stages.miniPlan: Feature order, transforms, architecture, weights, threshold.
stages.interactionPlan: Introduce a feature-order or scaling mismatch and trace its impact; restore the correct pipeline.
stages.reference: Save input names and order, units, shapes, fitted scales, category rules, architecture, activations, weights, software settings and decision policy. Validate required fields before prediction. Swapping input columns changes their meaning; missing a required field should be handled explicitly rather than silently guessed. The lab demonstrates these contract failures.

stages.title: Different network families organize information differently
stages.question: Why do different architectures exist?
stages.miniPlan: Tabular, image, and sequence structure.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a representation and show the relevant inductive assumption; avoid forcing every family into one tiny network diagram.
stages.reference: CNN means convolutional neural network: a filter uses products and sums across local inputs. RNN means recurrent neural network: each step updates a carried hidden state. Attention normalizes query–key scores into weights that combine value vectors. The diagrams show small local computations, not trained large language or image models. Compare their mechanics and requirements rather than treating one as universally best.

stages.title: Try the tiny student-pass network
stages.question: Can I predict this tiny network's answer?
stages.miniPlan: A fully numeric input-to-output calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Expose one controlled input/weight at a time; add a reset to the authored example and a computed receipt.
stages.reference: The plot shows the probability or decision for the current fitted network. Colours need the legend: activation colours are not the same as class-probability colours. Keep the inspected point fixed when comparing training updates. Manual parameter changes and actual gradient updates are distinct experiments.

stages.title: One full training cycle
stages.question: Can I explain a complete training cycle?
stages.miniPlan: One row or batch across all four learning operations.
stages.interactionPlan: Step, rewind, and replay once; end playback at completion and test that gradients precede weight updates.
stages.reference: Complete one cycle, inspect unchanged weights during forward/loss/gradient phases, then inspect the update. Rewind and repeat using the same starting snapshot. Record data splits, objective, settings, checkpoint rule and evaluation scope. A small teaching network illustrates mechanics; it does not establish real-world predictive reliability.

neural-networks.title: Neural Networks
neural-networks.intro: Follow a small network from inputs to prediction, error, gradients and update. See exactly which step changes the weights.
neural-networks.prerequisite: Multiplication, addition, fractions, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: What problem is One-R solving?
stages.question: What does one feature mean?
stages.miniPlan: Features versus target in one umbrella row.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a column and keep the target clearly separate.
stages.reference: A feature is an input column; the target is the answer to predict. In a separate 14-day umbrella example, candidate inputs are outlook, humidity, wind and temperature. One-R uses one of them at prediction time. It is a baseline, not a claim that one feature explains the whole outcome.

stages.title: First, make the lazy prediction.
stages.question: Why start with a majority baseline?
stages.miniPlan: 8 Yes / 6 No → 8 of 14 correct.
stages.interactionPlan: Predict the baseline before revealing it; add an imbalanced case where accuracy is misleading.
stages.reference: In the separate example, 8 Yes and 6 No rows give a Yes-for-everyone training accuracy of 8/14. With 70 Yes and 30 No, the baseline predicts Yes and gets 70%. If a rare class matters, accuracy alone is not enough to judge usefulness.

stages.title: Build a rule for each group of input values.
stages.question: How is a rule built for each value?
stages.miniPlan: Value-level class counts and majority.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a category and trace its chosen prediction and errors.
stages.reference: For Outlook=Sunny, collect those training rows, count Yes and No, then save the more common answer. Repeat for Cloudy and Rainy. Errors for a value are rows disagreeing with its saved class. The same method applies to numeric intervals. Ties require a fixed rule rather than a choice made to improve the reported result.
stages.experiment: Choose input x or z. Count the class dots in each interval and read its saved class. Move that input to another interval and follow the gold mark to the returned answer.

stages.title: Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule.
stages.question: How is the winning feature selected?
stages.miniPlan: Competing feature rulebooks and training errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect each feature without changing rows; reveal the declared tie policy.
stages.reference: The separate example has Outlook 3/14 errors, Humidity 4/14, and Wind and bucketed Temperature 5/14. Fitting chooses the smallest training-error rule under stated tie rules. This fitting comparison is not an unbiased estimate of the selected rule's future performance. Refitting selection inside held-out evaluation assesses the whole procedure.

stages.title: Turn numeric values into intervals.
stages.question: Why bucket numeric values?
stages.miniPlan: Exact-value lookup versus training-derived intervals.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query through fixed intervals; explain that exact-value rules can memorize the sample.
stages.reference: A separate teaching rule uses Temperature≤22.5, 22.5<Temperature≤27.5, and Temperature>27.5. Exact cut procedures vary by implementation. Do not inspect test labels to improve them. Saving the cut points gives a reproducible rule for new temperatures such as 23.6 rather than memorizing every exact training value.

stages.title: Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model.
stages.question: What happens with missing or unseen values?
stages.miniPlan: Missing, unseen category, tie, out-of-range cases.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose an edge case and trace the declared fallback; do not infer a rule from test labels.
stages.reference: If Outlook=Hazy never appeared in training, apply the saved fallback. Missing is not automatically an observed category unless the procedure defines it that way. Numeric values outside the training range also need a rule. These choices are part of the fitted procedure, not decisions improvised from an evaluation row.
stages.experiment: Choose Missing value for the selected rule input. Watch the model use its saved training-majority fallback. Restore Measured value and compare the interval rule.

stages.title: Prediction is deliberately cheap.
stages.question: Why is prediction inexpensive?
stages.miniPlan: Read feature → find category → return rule.
stages.interactionPlan: Change irrelevant input fields and show the prediction stays unchanged for the fitted one-feature model.
stages.reference: If Outlook wins, a Cloudy row may look up Yes while humidity and wind are ignored. That means Outlook gave the best single-column fit among the candidates under this procedure. It does not mean the other columns have no information or causal relevance. Prediction applies the saved table without reselecting the feature.

stages.title: One feature cannot express an interaction.
stages.question: What can a single feature miss?
stages.miniPlan: A two-feature interaction table.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal a pattern that requires both features and compare One-R with a richer rule.
stages.reference: XOR is a simple interaction: the class is positive when exactly one of two binary inputs is 1. Each input alone may tell little, while the pair determines the answer. A one-column lookup cannot capture that full rule. An interpretable feature can also be a proxy for another factor; readability is not evidence of causality or suitability.
stages.experiment: Choose Inner and outer rings. Move both input coordinates and compare the background decisions with the known point labels. Can a rule reading only one coordinate describe the whole two-coordinate ring pattern?

stages.title: Validate the whole learning process
stages.question: What must be refitted inside each fold?
stages.miniPlan: Buckets, feature selection, value rules, and scoring.
stages.interactionPlan: Step a fold with training-only learning; show why selecting a feature globally leaks selection information.
stages.reference: For every fold, learn preparation and rules on the training part, freeze them, then predict the held-out part. Keep repeated people, devices or organizations together when the deployment question requires new groups. Otherwise the model may recognize a group rather than generalize to a genuinely new one.

stages.title: Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next.
stages.question: Which metric matches the decision?
stages.miniPlan: Actual denominators and concrete FP/FN costs.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fold outcomes and workload; avoid tying entire industries universally to precision or recall.
stages.reference: Precision asks how often alerts are correct; recall asks how many actual positives are found. Report fold scores, their average and spread, and compare the baseline on the same splits. Fold models share training rows, so their SD is not automatically a confidence interval. There are no universal percentage bands that say a model is stable enough to deploy.

stages.title: Use simple models as diagnostic instruments.
stages.question: How does One-R differ from a stump?
stages.miniPlan: Majority baseline / categorical One-R / one split / full tree.
stages.interactionPlan: Run the same row through each representation and explain the tradeoff.
stages.reference: One-R uses one feature but may map many of its values to different classes. A numeric stump makes one cutoff; categorical stump behavior depends on the split implementation. A full tree can make later questions depend on earlier answers. If one feature nearly matches a complex model, check useful signal and possible leakage rather than assuming either explanation.

stages.title: Build the rule, then explain what it means.
stages.question: Can I build and explain a rule?
stages.miniPlan: A partially completed value-level rulebook.
stages.interactionPlan: Complete a rule, test a new case, and explain what the unselected features might still contribute elsewhere.
stages.reference: Trace input value, interval, stored vote, fallback if needed and final class. Show the training error used to select the feature separately from validation performance. Explain the limitation to one input, chosen tie policy, missing-value policy and evaluation split. Good explanation does not replace good evidence.

one-r.title: One-R
one-r.intro: Build an easy-to-read rule using one input column. Compare its value-by-value votes with a simple majority baseline.
one-r.prerequisite: Counting, fractions, and the training/validation distinction.

stages.title: The Unsupervised Explorer
stages.question: What can we learn without a target?
stages.miniPlan: Rows, six features, and the absence of a y column.
stages.interactionPlan: Select one student across the source table and 2D slice; label the slice versus the full fit.
stages.reference: The live example has eight observations and two features. Centre each column by subtracting its average. Sample covariance is XᵀX/(n−1) for the centred table X. Eigenvectors are the component directions; eigenvalues are their score variances. These names describe the calculation, not a guarantee that the directions are scientifically meaningful.

stages.title: The "Too Much Information" Problem
stages.question: Why compress several measurements?
stages.miniPlan: Original point and projections on two candidate axes.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare reconstruction loss after discarding a direction; avoid equating sample variance with all information.
stages.reference: With six inputs there are 15 pairwise plots; with ten there are 45. PCA gives new combined coordinates rather than pretending one old axis shows everything. Correlated inputs can share information, but small-variance directions may still matter. Compression should be chosen for a stated purpose.

stages.title: Finding the First Principal Component
stages.question: Why maximize projected variance?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate direction, projected spread, reconstruction error.
stages.interactionPlan: Rotate a candidate axis continuously and mark the fitted PC1 optimum; use a centered dataset.
stages.reference: Projection assigns each centred point a position on the candidate unit-length line. PCA maximizes the variance of those positions. Equivalently, it minimizes squared perpendicular reconstruction distance to that line. This equivalence concerns the chosen centred numeric scale and squared error, not all kinds of information or distance.

stages.title: The Secret Sauce: Loadings
stages.question: What are loadings?
stages.miniPlan: One score as a weighted sum of standardized features.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a loading, highlight the source column, and trace its contribution for one student.
stages.reference: A component score is the sum of loading×centred input contributions. If scaling is selected, use the scaled inputs instead. Directions have unit length and are perpendicular. Reversing every loading and score sign produces the same reconstruction, so signs alone do not establish a uniquely positive or negative scientific factor.
stages.experiment: Read the two fitted PC1 weights. Change the input units or standardization. Predict how the fitted weights change; the free trial angle is not used here.

stages.title: When Scaling Is Appropriate
stages.question: Why might scaling change the answer?
stages.miniPlan: Raw units, mean, SD, centered value, z-score.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch raw-centered and standardized fits on identical rows; retain units and model-choice explanation.
stages.reference: Standardization subtracts the training mean and divides by the training SD. It puts variables on a comparable relative-spread scale. If units differ, this may be useful; if common-unit variance differences carry meaning, it may be unwanted. Zero-spread columns need explicit handling. Fit any scaler and PCA only on training data for a predictive evaluation.

stages.title: Capturing the Leftovers: PC2
stages.question: How is PC2 selected?
stages.miniPlan: Remaining variation after PC1 with an orthogonality constraint.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the second eigen-direction; distinguish PCA score decorrelation from arbitrary perpendicular axes.
stages.reference: Perpendicular means at 90 degrees. In the fitted sample covariance, component scores are uncorrelated. This does not generally mean independent or causally unrelated. Later population data need not have exactly the same fitted covariance. A second direction is chosen for remaining variance, not for an outcome label.
stages.experiment: Keep standardization off and change z measurement units. Watch both fitted axes change while staying at right angles. Then standardize and compare the effect of changing units.

stages.title: The Transformation (Scores)
stages.question: What are scores?
stages.miniPlan: One original row versus its new coordinates.
stages.interactionPlan: Animate coordinates into the new basis with identity preserved; show reconstruction when all components are kept.
stages.reference: Keeping all components can reconstruct centred inputs up to numerical precision. Keeping fewer leaves reconstruction gaps. Scores are new row coordinates, not model probabilities. Loadings are direction weights, not rows. Inspect original and reconstructed coordinates for the same selected observation.
