stages.experiment: Choose an observation. Follow its gold ring in the fitted PC1/PC2 plot and read those two fitted scores in the receipt. Compare these new coordinates with the same row’s prepared input coordinates.

stages.title: Proportion of Variance Explained
stages.question: What fraction of variance is retained?
stages.miniPlan: Eigenvalue / total eigenvalue and cumulative PVE.
stages.interactionPlan: Select component count on a scree plot; distinguish variance retained from predictive information preserved.
stages.reference: The scree bars show component variances or their ratios; the cumulative line adds retained sample variance. An elbow can help describe the pattern, but does not prove a best component count. A low-variance component can still predict an important target. Discarding components only reduces noise when those directions actually contain mostly noise.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: Can I discover the best projection?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate-angle score compared with fitted PCA.
stages.interactionPlan: Give a predict/try/reveal exercise; do not call every user-selected axis a principal component.
stages.reference: Use the same points and scale while rotating the trial direction. Compare the measured variance with the fitted maximum and inspect each point's reconstruction gap. In two inputs, the perpendicular second axis completes the rotation. Do not assume the widest-looking view preserves every useful detail.

stages.title: The Best Summary
stages.question: What should I report and avoid claiming?
stages.miniPlan: Scaling, component count, loadings, PVE, and limitations.
stages.interactionPlan: Explain a chosen representation; include a low-variance predictive-signal counterexample in deeper reading.
stages.reference: State which data fitted the means, scales and component directions. Report component count, loadings, explained variance, selection rule and any downstream validation. PCA is unsupervised, but it can still leak evaluation inputs if fitted before a predictive split. Frozen training parameters should transform later rows unchanged.
stages.experiment: Keep one component, then keep two. Watch the green reconstruction rings meet the original points and the total squared gaps become zero.

pca.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
pca.intro: Rotate the view of numeric data and keep fewer coordinates. See exactly which variation stays and which variation is lost.
pca.prerequisite: Averages, two-axis plots, and the idea of squared spread.

stages.title: Inspect the Raw Data
stages.question: Why might a straight line miss the pattern?
stages.miniPlan: Three local regions of a curved dataset.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight systematic residual patterns using the same points; begin with a question rather than declaring linear methods inadequate.
stages.reference: The model is linear in its coefficients even when its graph curves in x. For degree 2, ŷ=b₀+b₁x+b₂x². A valley or hill may be easier to represent than with one line. A polynomial is one possible curve family, not the only option.

stages.title: Fit a Straight Line
stages.question: What does a baseline teach us?
stages.miniPlan: Baseline prediction and observed value.
stages.interactionPlan: Fit degree one and reveal residual structure; state that polynomial regression remains linear in its coefficients.
stages.reference: Underfitting means the model misses important structure because its allowed shape is too restricted. A straight line can be a useful baseline even when it misses a curve. Compare errors on the same observations and evaluation plan. A poor baseline does not prove any more complex model will succeed.

stages.title: Expand the Features
stages.question: Why create x-squared and x-cubed?
stages.miniPlan: One raw x transformed into basis columns.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush a row across the raw table and design matrix; label training-fitted centering/scaling.
stages.reference: For x=3, the new columns are x=3, x²=9 and x³=27. The rows still refer to the same observations. A design matrix is the table of these model columns. Scaling and centring can improve numerical stability before building powers. Learn any such transformation on training data only.

stages.title: Fit the Weights
stages.question: What do the weights do?
stages.miniPlan: Signed basis contribution bars.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle individual basis terms and their sum; update the full equation without swapping the dataset.
stages.reference: The prediction adds all basis terms. A basis function is an ingredient such as x². A one-unit change in x changes several ingredients at once, so b₂ alone is not a constant overall slope. Closely related powers can make coefficient estimates unstable. Inspect the combined prediction and uncertainty.

stages.title: Compute Errors
stages.question: What do residual patterns tell us?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction → error → squared error.
stages.interactionPlan: Link a residual plot point with its original observation; preserve the training/validation distinction.
stages.reference: Residuals reveal what the fitted mean did not capture. A curve suggests a missing mean pattern; a funnel suggests unequal error variance. Neither shape identifies the cause by itself. Low training MSE does not prove that predictions on new data are reliable.

stages.title: Check for Overfitting
stages.question: Why can a flexible curve do worse on new data?
stages.miniPlan: Same degree with train and validation errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub degree on a fixed split; highlight boundary oscillation and label any schematic curve.
stages.reference: Adding many degrees can make training SSE small while validation error grows. That is one sign of overfitting. Real error curves can be irregular rather than a perfect U-shape. A polynomial can change dramatically outside the measured range, called extrapolation. The live gold validation points are for development; they are not an untouched final test.

stages.title: Find the Sweet Spot
stages.question: How should we select the degree?
stages.miniPlan: Near-best validation candidates with complexity.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidate degrees using fixed folds or a fixed holdout; noise regeneration must be explicit.
stages.reference: Use the same folds to compare candidates, with scaling and feature building fitted inside each training fold. Compare scores, uncertainty and stability instead of chasing a tiny lead. Prefer the simplest useful procedure when nearby choices perform similarly, with the tie rule stated in advance.

stages.title: Lock in the Model
stages.question: What gets locked before final evaluation?
stages.miniPlan: Basis, transforms, degree, coefficients, and threshold if relevant.
stages.interactionPlan: Commit the chosen setup, reveal final test once, and explain extrapolation/monitoring limits instead of claiming proof.
stages.reference: Freeze all learned preparation, degree, regularization, coefficients or final refitting rule, and evaluation metric. Test on independent observations relevant to deployment. Report sample size, error and limitations such as extrapolation or a changed data distribution. If the test result drives new choices, obtain fresh evidence for the revised model.

polynomial-regression.title: Polynomial Regression
polynomial-regression.intro: Give a regression model room to bend. Compare useful curves with curves that only follow training noise.
polynomial-regression.prerequisite: Simple Linear Regression and prediction errors.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why does a sample answer vary?
stages.miniPlan: Population, sample, statistic, and parameter in four labeled positions.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw one explicit sample and show its mean; retain the population as the stable reference.
stages.reference: A parameter is a fixed number describing the chosen population, such as its true mean. A statistic is a number calculated from a sample. Before selecting the sample, that statistic can take different values. Repeating the same sampling method helps show how much it varies. It does not change the population parameter.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: How are probability, density, and frequency different?
stages.miniPlan: Discrete mass versus continuous interval area.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an interval and accumulate area; do not interpret continuous curve height as point probability.
stages.reference: P(A | B) means the chance of A among cases where B happened: P(A ∩ B)/P(B), when P(B)>0. The ∩ symbol means both events. Independence means knowing B does not change A's chance, so P(A ∩ B)=P(A)P(B). Expectation E[X] is an average weighted by probabilities. Variance E[(X−E[X])²] is the average squared gap from that average, when these quantities exist. Density uses area, and its height may exceed 1.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How is a standard error calculated?
stages.miniPlan: SD, n, square root of n, and SE with units.
stages.interactionPlan: Work one numerical example; contrast individual-score spread with mean-estimate spread.
stages.reference: For SD 12 and n = 36, √36 = 6 because 6×6 = 36. Estimated SE = 12/6 = 2. This uses the independent-sampling formula. Four times the sample size doubles the square root, so it halves SE. Using the sample SD makes this an estimate, not an exactly known population SE.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: What is the sampling distribution?
stages.miniPlan: One sample produces one dot in a distribution of means.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the population → sample → mean chain before showing hundreds of means; explain CLT conditions in deeper reading.
stages.reference: The population plot shows individual values. The second plot shows one statistic from each sample. Its spread depends on the population, sample size, chosen statistic and sampling method. The central limit theorem often helps approximate sample means with a bell curve as sample size grows. It does not make every small or heavy-tailed sample normal. Weights, clustering and sampling much of a finite population can change the usual SE formula.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What changes with sample size?
stages.miniPlan: Fixed seed, sample size, repeat count, and theoretical SE.
stages.interactionPlan: Generate samples outside draw; resize without resampling; animate added means and offer an explicit resample action.
stages.reference: Increasing the sample size makes each mean steadier. Increasing the number of simulation repeats makes our picture of that distribution clearer. These are different changes. More repeats do not reduce the uncertainty of a mean calculated from a sample of the same size.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: When is the usual SE misleading?
stages.miniPlan: Independent versus clustered observations.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare samples with the same row count but different dependence; explain heavy-tail and design limits.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Repeated samples must follow the stated population and sampling design. The simple SD/√n formula assumes independent information; related observations need a suitable adjustment.

When the method fails

Repeating a sampling claim assumes the same population and method each time. A group of related observations, called a cluster, may carry less information than the same number of independent people. Skewed distributions and frequent extreme values can need larger samples or other methods. A convenience sample does not become representative just by getting bigger.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: Which sampling design matches the question?
stages.miniPlan: Population frame, selection, weighting, and estimator.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a simple sampling workflow with a bias scenario; separate random sampling from random assignment.
stages.reference: The sampling frame is the list or group that could be selected. Check who it leaves out. A random variable describes a measurement whose value is not yet known. Choose the sampling method, statistic and any weights, then assess its sampling distribution and SE. Random assignment among volunteers does not make those volunteers a random sample of everyone.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should a sampling result report?
stages.miniPlan: Estimate, design, n, SE/interval, and limitations.
stages.interactionPlan: Fill a short report from the actual sample state; identify the population to which it refers.
stages.reference: What to report: State the target population, who could enter, how selection happened, sample size, statistic, related groups or repeated records, and the uncertainty method. Small SE describes little sampling variation under those assumptions. It does not rule out selection bias, poor measurements or missing coverage.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I tell SD from SE?
stages.miniPlan: One short classification task plus a missing calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Mix answer positions and explain every distractor; retain static answers and a new numerical transfer example.
stages.reference: For SD 8 and n 16, estimated SE = 8/√16 = 8/4 = 2 under independent sampling. SD remains the spread of individuals. SE is the spread of the mean estimator. Always say which quantity a dot, interval or histogram describes.

probability-sampling.title: Probability & Sampling Distributions
probability-sampling.intro: A different sample can give a different answer. See what changes, how much it changes, and why bigger samples often help.
probability-sampling.prerequisite: Averages, fractions, and reading a histogram.

stages.title: The Raw Data Cloud
stages.question: What differs between these class clouds?
stages.miniPlan: Class size, center, spread, and tilt.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect classes with stable row IDs and color/shape labels.
stages.reference: QDA is a supervised classifier: fitting uses known class labels. Its usual model gives each class a multivariate Gaussian, or bell-shaped cloud in several inputs. Equal-density contours describe the model, not physical fruit boundaries. The highest posterior, meaning class probability after seeing the inputs, supplies the usual label decision.

stages.title: Keep training, validation and test separate
stages.question: Why hold out examples?
stages.miniPlan: Training estimates versus validation comparisons versus final test.
stages.interactionPlan: Use immutable split roles; keep subsequent shape/regularization tuning on development data.
stages.reference: Do not use validation or test rows to calculate fitted centres, shapes or training-derived priors. Keep each evaluation row out of the model used to predict it. Tune any stabilization using development data. The toy proportions are teaching choices, not a required 80/20 rule for every study.

stages.title: The Straight-Line Trap (LDA)
stages.question: When is a straight boundary too restrictive?
stages.miniPlan: One ambiguous point under shared and separate covariance.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare LDA/QDA on the same points; avoid implying QDA always improves generalization.
stages.reference: LDA pools within-class spread, rather than forcing the full raw dataset into one grand-centred covariance. QDA compares separate class shapes. More flexibility is not automatically better: a curved fit to noise may predict worse than a straight rule. Compare on rows outside fitting.

stages.title: Fitting QDA: What the Model Learns
stages.question: Which parameters does QDA estimate?
stages.miniPlan: Prior, mean, covariance; matrix entries with units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a matrix cell to highlight ellipse spread/tilt; explain determinant volume and inverse scaling separately.
stages.reference: For two features, covariance is a 2×2 table. The diagonal gives each feature's variance; the off-diagonal gives their linear co-movement. μ is the centre and Σ the covariance. The determinant |Σ| measures covariance volume scaling; √|Σ| relates to geometric area or volume. Σ⁻¹ adjusts distances for shape. Too few independent rows or redundant inputs can make the inverse unavailable or unstable.

stages.title: Testing with Shape-Aware Distance
stages.question: What is shape-aware distance?
stages.miniPlan: Euclidean versus Mahalanobis distance for one query.
stages.interactionPlan: Move the query by pointer or coordinate inputs; show contours and the computed class terms.
stages.reference: Straight-line Euclidean distance does not itself assume classes are circles. It just ignores class-specific spread and tilt. QDA's score also includes −½log|Σ_k| and log prior, not only distance. A broad cloud spreads its density over more space. Model probabilities rely on the fitted distributional assumptions and may be poorly calibrated if those assumptions miss important structure.

stages.title: The Curved Boundary
stages.question: Why do unequal covariance shapes yield a quadratic boundary?
stages.miniPlan: Shared versus nonshared quadratic terms.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle linear/quadratic boundaries with direct labels; distinguish geometric shape from a confidence claim.
stages.reference: The score is −½log|Σ_k| −½(x−μ_k)ᵀΣ_k⁻¹(x−μ_k)+log(π_k), apart from terms shared by classes. At the boundary the scores tie. Shared covariance cancels the quadratic part, giving LDA. Different covariances can retain it. Special cases may still have straight or disconnected boundaries, so do not assume every QDA boundary is one smooth enclosing curve.

stages.title: Evaluating QDA on Unseen Data
stages.question: How should performance be evaluated while exploring?
stages.miniPlan: One confusion-cell calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Display validation metrics while tuning; reserve test for locked settings and remove advice to repeatedly inspect changing test scores.
stages.reference: Pick error measures for the task and keep evaluation roles clear. Thresholds, priors and regularization are development choices. A false positive predicts the designated positive class for an actual negative. The small validation display illustrates these counts; it does not establish final-test or production performance.

stages.title: Reading QDA Output
stages.question: What do prior and covariance outputs mean?
stages.miniPlan: Output item → source data → interpretation.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus/tap the log/table entries; state whether priors came from training frequencies or were supplied.
stages.reference: A prior of .70 assigns the class a 70% baseline before using the new row's measurements. It is not the fraction the model must predict as that class. Combine the prior with class likelihoods to obtain posterior probabilities. Priors estimated in one population may not suit a later population with different class frequencies.

stages.title: Regularization & Shape Playground
stages.question: What does regularization stabilize?
stages.miniPlan: Identity ridge versus pooled-covariance shrinkage.
stages.interactionPlan: Give separate controls or separate demonstrations; only the pooled path should be labeled as moving toward LDA.
stages.reference: Pooled shrinkage mixes each class covariance with the same pooled covariance. That creates a path towards shared shapes and LDA in this lab. Adding a small identity-matrix term mainly helps make the inverse usable; it does not usually make unequal class shapes equal. Name the target and select the amount using validation. Different software may implement a different target.

stages.title: Assumptions, Complexity & Synthesis
stages.question: When is the extra flexibility worth its cost?
stages.miniPlan: Parameter count by K and p with required sample support.
stages.interactionPlan: Change K/p and inspect covariance stability; conclude with a validation-based choice, not a shape-only rule.
stages.reference: For K classes and p features, separate symmetric covariances use K×p(p+1)/2 entries. LDA uses one set of p(p+1)/2 instead. Both also estimate class means and priors. For two classes and two features, the usual free-parameter totals are 10 for QDA and 7 for LDA. More parameters can require more representative data. Compare useful performance, calibration, stability and resource cost under the same evaluation plan.

qda.title: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA)
qda.intro: Let each labelled group have its own centre, spread and tilt. See why separate shapes can create a curved decision boundary.
qda.prerequisite: Two-axis plots and LDA’s class means and covariance shapes.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why combine several trees?
stages.miniPlan: One unstable tree versus an average/vote.
stages.interactionPlan: Perturb one training sample and compare variability of single-tree and ensemble predictions.
stages.reference: One tree's greedy cuts can change sharply after a small data change. Varied trees can average out some of that movement. They still share the original training dataset, so hundreds of trees are not hundreds of independent datasets. Averaging is useful under appropriate diversity; it does not guarantee lower error in every case.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What makes trees different?
stages.miniPlan: Bootstrap rows and random candidate features.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal one tree's sample and a node's feature subset; distinguish row sampling from feature sampling.
stages.reference: Replacement means a row remains available after every draw. One tree may see the same original row several times and omit another. Random candidate features change which questions it can consider at each split. These two mechanisms are distinct, and both affect tree diversity.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How is a forest prediction produced?
stages.miniPlan: Three trees' votes or numeric predictions.
stages.interactionPlan: Accumulate one selected row's tree outputs; compute the aggregate directly.
stages.reference: For regression, average the tree numbers. For this classifier, average leaf class-1 fractions, then apply the cutoff. As a separate example, fractions .6,.6,.01 average to about .403, while two of three hard .5-cutoff votes are positive. Name the aggregation rule because hard voting and averaged probabilities need not agree.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Why does correlation between trees matter?
stages.miniPlan: Independent versus highly similar prediction errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare averaging behavior under clearly labeled scenarios; keep bias and variance separate.
stages.reference: Compare predictions on the same validation points. Near-diagonal points in a two-tree comparison mean the predictions are similar; shared mistakes matter too. Correlation describes how their outputs move together, not proof of independence. More trees mainly reduce finite-forest randomness. Reducing feature candidates too much can weaken individual trees.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What is an out-of-bag prediction?
stages.miniPlan: In-bag membership across trees for one observation.
stages.interactionPlan: Compute votes only from trees that omitted the row; replace the current stylized OOB error curve if it remains labeled measured error.
stages.reference: OOB means out of bag. For a row, exclude every tree whose bootstrap sample included it, even once. Average only the eligible trees. If there are none, the estimate is unavailable rather than zero. OOB is development evidence; heavy tuning against it can still require outer evaluation.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What problems do more trees not solve?
stages.miniPlan: Leakage, biased sampling, drift, and unreliable importance.
stages.interactionPlan: Show an ensemble agreeing on a wrong shortcut; explain permutation importance with correlated predictors.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Training and evaluation must represent the intended use. Inputs must be available at prediction time, and related groups or time must be split appropriately.

When the method fails

Forests can rely on accidental information, extrapolate poorly in regression, or predict probabilities needing calibration. Inputs must be available at prediction time and evaluation must respect related groups or time. Feature importance measures predictive behavior under a specified method, not causation. Correlated inputs can substitute for each other.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should a forest be tuned and validated?
stages.miniPlan: Leaf size, feature subset, class weights, OOB/CV, final test.
stages.interactionPlan: Tune on development estimates and compare to a baseline; do not treat OOB as an unlimited unbiased tuning resource.
stages.reference: Tune leaf constraints and feature sampling under suitable validation. Grow enough trees for sufficiently stable results, rather than treating a larger count as a cure. Keep learned preparation within resampling. Check useful errors, calibration, subgroups and resource cost. Lock the selected procedure before final evaluation.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should be reported?
stages.miniPlan: Evaluation design, parameters, class metrics, calibration, and importance limits.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a forest summary with explicit predictive rather than causal interpretation.
stages.reference: What to report: State tree count, seed, feature sampling, depth and leaf limits, split design, OOB use and aggregation. Give sample sizes, relevant metrics, uncertainty and limitations. Permutation importance measures the effect of disrupting an input on a chosen score; impurity importance is a different measure. Neither is a causal ranking of variables.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I trace a kept-out vote?
stages.miniPlan: A row present in some bootstrap samples and absent in others.
stages.interactionPlan: Select the valid OOB voters and compute the result; give feedback explaining excluded trees.
stages.reference: Inspect the row's actual bootstrap membership. Crossed-out trees used that row and cannot supply its OOB prediction. A fraction based on few eligible trees can be variable. OOB does not mean a completely separate new dataset; it is a held-out prediction assembled from parts of the training resampling process.

random-forest.title: Random Forest
random-forest.intro: Combine varied trees and follow how their predictions are averaged. See which trees may fairly vote on each training row.
random-forest.prerequisite: Decision trees, averages, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why can a high R-squared coexist with a bad model?
stages.miniPlan: Similar summary score, different residual patterns.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare two labeled examples on equal axes and ask which model claim is unsupported.
stages.reference: A model can return a number for every row even when its shape or uncertainty assumptions are poor. Diagnostics are checks, not automatic pass/fail proofs. Inspect the raw data, fitted predictions, residuals, sampling design and intended use together.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What is a residual checking?
stages.miniPlan: Actual − fitted value, with one row.
stages.interactionPlan: Link raw plot, fitted value, and residual plot by observation ID.
stages.reference: For actual 61 and predicted 65, residual is −4. The prediction was four units too high. A cloud around zero without a clear curve is reassuring about mean form, but is not a complete model assessment. Residual plots use outcome units; they are not new input measurements.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How does an influential point differ from an outlier?
stages.miniPlan: Residual size, leverage, and coefficient change.
stages.interactionPlan: Remove/restore a selected point in a controlled comparison; do not prescribe automatic deletion.
stages.reference: Unusual inputs can have leverage even if their residual is small. Influence concerns what changes when that observation is perturbed or left out. A separate salary example with errors around ±5k for junior staff and ±40k for senior staff shows unequal spread, not necessarily one bad row. Ordinary uncertainty calculations may need robust errors or an explicit variance model.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Which diagnostic answers which question?
stages.miniPlan: Residual/fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage, and VIF.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus one diagnostic at a time with a question and response; distinguish predictor normality from residual inference assumptions.
stages.reference: A residual-versus-fitted plot checks pattern and spread. A Q–Q plot compares ordered residuals with a reference such as a normal distribution. Normal predictors are not required just because a test uses normal errors. Cook's distance screens influence, not automatic deletion. VIF measures how much a predictor overlaps the others; it can help explain wide coefficient intervals without proving bias.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What does a curve or funnel suggest?
stages.miniPlan: Healthy/curved/fanning residual thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a pattern with a stable dataset; link a possible remedy to a refit, labeled illustrative if no fit occurs.
stages.reference: Curvature may suggest another mean function or missing input. A funnel may suggest a variance model or robust uncertainty method. A data error needs correction; a real extreme case may need retention and a sensitivity comparison. Evaluate a justified repair on suitable new data.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What cannot a residual plot establish?
stages.miniPlan: Independence from design, causal validity, and limited sample power.
stages.interactionPlan: Show a time/group violation even when the scatter looks harmless.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Check the mean form and error structure needed by your chosen analysis. Independent errors, equal spread and normal errors are assumptions of particular classical methods, not properties proved by a plot.

When the method fails

Repeated people, time dependence or groups can give related errors even in an ordinary-looking scatterplot. Normal-error assumptions matter for some classical small-sample inference, not for every use of a regression prediction. Constant variance is also an assumption of particular uncertainty methods, not proof supplied by a tidy plot.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should a diagnostic change the analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Symptom → investigate → justified model change → validate.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a response and compare outcomes; retain the original dataset and model for sensitivity analysis.
stages.reference: Document the original model and the changed version. Explain which issue the change addresses. Check residuals again and compare estimates, intervals and held-out errors. Changes chosen after inspecting data are exploratory choices and need appropriately honest evaluation.

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should the report say?
stages.miniPlan: Finding, changed assumption/model, sensitivity, and resulting uncertainty.
stages.interactionPlan: Assemble a short diagnostic note; distinguish a confidence interval from a prediction interval.
stages.reference: What to report: Report coefficients with units and intervals, residual standard error, diagnostic findings and justified sensitivity results. A confidence interval for a mean response describes the estimated average. A prediction interval for a new outcome also includes individual variation and is usually wider under the same model.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I match symptom and response?
stages.miniPlan: A novel plot and a choice of scientifically justified actions.
stages.interactionPlan: Require a reason before reveal; include a keep-and-investigate answer rather than always delete or transform.
stages.reference: Do not remove an observation just because it lowers R² or prevents a small p-value. Verify measurements and inclusion rules. Explain any excluded cases, transformations, dependence handling and remaining limits. The scientific question decides whether a change is useful.

regression-diagnostics.title: Regression Diagnostics
regression-diagnostics.intro: Look at what the model missed. Use error plots to ask better questions before trusting a fitted line.
regression-diagnostics.prerequisite: Simple Linear Regression, residuals, and reading a scatterplot.

stages.title: The Raw Target
stages.question: What are we predicting?
stages.miniPlan: One home's features and numeric price.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the row to the plotted house; keep outcome units on axes and prediction labels.
stages.reference: A node is one group of training rows. An internal node asks a question; a leaf gives a number. The live model uses the inputs and outcome units on its axes. A house-price example is an analogy, not the live dataset. The plotted region and branching diagram describe the same fitted tree and selected point.

stages.title: From Dataset to Model
stages.question: Which rows can influence training?
stages.miniPlan: Train/validation/test role cards with immutable IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal membership without allowing test outcomes to guide splits.
stages.reference: The target is the number to predict. Features are inputs known at prediction time. Training fits the tree. Validation evaluates development choices. A final test evaluates the locked procedure. Keep any learned preparation inside training, and split related people or time periods appropriately.

stages.title: The Clumsy Guess
stages.question: Why start with the mean?
stages.miniPlan: Three target values, their mean, and squared errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidate constant predictions and locate the minimum RSS at the mean.
stages.reference: For squared error, the best constant is the mean. Move a trial constant away from that mean and total squared gaps grow. The root average is a baseline, not a prediction that every outcome really equals that value. Calculate it from the current training rows. It changes when those rows change.

stages.title: The First Split
stages.question: How can one question improve the prediction?
stages.miniPlan: Left and right child counts and means.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide a split and show piecewise-constant predictions; keep equality routing explicit.
stages.reference: This notebook sends values equal to the cutoff to the left: x≤cutoff. The other side uses x>cutoff. Each child mean uses only its own training rows. In two inputs, the cut spans the current parent's region, not every unrelated branch's region.

stages.title: The Error Engine (RSS)
stages.question: How is a split scored?
stages.miniPlan: Parent RSS minus left RSS minus right RSS.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a candidate threshold and trace both children's contributions to total improvement.
stages.reference: SSE, also called RSS here, is the sum of squared residuals. Split improvement = parent SSE − (left SSE + right SSE). A child-variance average must be weighted by child sizes to correspond to this total. A low training score is not yet evidence about new-data prediction.

stages.title: Real Trees Check Many Questions
stages.question: Why test many candidate questions?
stages.miniPlan: Feature/threshold/RSS ranking table.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through adjacent-value midpoint candidates; keep ties deterministic and explain greedy search.
stages.reference: For each feature, sort the distinct values and examine midpoint cutoffs. Leaf-size and other rules can reject a candidate. Greedy means best at the current node, not best across every complete future tree. Compare the gold candidate with the measured minimum on the displayed feature's cost curve.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.question: What makes the process recursive?
stages.miniPlan: The same split recipe reused in one child.
stages.interactionPlan: Expand one node at a time and update its spatial region; keep other nodes stable.
stages.reference: Each child repeats the search using only the rows inside that child. The tree stops at its depth or sample limits, a constant outcome group, or no valid useful split. Different branches may stop at different levels. An added cut affects that local region and the corresponding branching path.

stages.title: The Anatomy of a Tree
stages.question: How do I read a tree?
stages.miniPlan: Root, question, branch, leaf, prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace one selected house through both tree and feature space, with keyboard step controls.
stages.reference: One query is the point we want to predict. Its input values choose a branch at every node. The highlighted region, path and leaf mean must agree. The leaf's sample size matters: a prediction based on very few rows can be unstable.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.question: Why can a deeper tree overfit?
stages.miniPlan: Leaf sizes and train/validation error comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Increase depth on a fixed dataset; show tiny leaves without revealing final test metrics.
stages.reference: Growing very deep may isolate rows when suitable splits exist, but does not always achieve zero error when identical inputs have different outcomes or growth rules constrain it. More depth improves allowed training fit, not necessarily validation. Real validation curves need not have one clean turning point.

stages.title: Stopping Rules
stages.question: Which stopping rules constrain growth?
stages.miniPlan: Maximum depth versus minimum leaf size.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one rule at a time and explain which proposed split becomes invalid.
stages.reference: max_depth limits path length. min_samples_leaf requires enough rows in each child. These are settings, not scientific constants. Compare the same candidate fits under suitable validation. If useful performance is similar, a stated simpler-model preference can be reasonable; it is not a universal law.

stages.title: Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back
stages.question: How does pruning differ from stopping early?
stages.miniPlan: Full subtree versus pruned leaf and its penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub a pruning path; keep validation-based selection separate from training cost complexity.
stages.reference: Cost-complexity pruning trades fitted training risk against the number of leaves. The α setting increases the cost of keeping branches. The live pruning comparison starts from one fixed grown tree, so it removes existing branches rather than secretly regrowing a different one. Choose α using development data.

stages.title: Trees vs. Lines
stages.question: When does a tree differ from a line?
stages.miniPlan: Smooth additive trend versus stepwise prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare both fits on identical observations and splits; avoid implying one always wins.
stages.reference: Hold the other input fixed when comparing a line-model slice with tree steps. The original observations still have their own second-input values. A smooth truth does not guarantee the line wins; model form, data and evaluation matter. Leaf-mean regression trees predict within the training outcome range and do not extrapolate a new trend.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: What changes when I alter the data?
stages.miniPlan: Before/after prediction for one selected house.
stages.interactionPlan: Preserve a baseline snapshot while changing noise or size; announce an explicit new experiment.
stages.reference: Compare the same query before and after a controlled change. A small outcome change can move a greedy root cut and alter later regions. Do not confuse that data sensitivity with changing the query itself. State which data or setting changed.

stages.title: Sample Output: Reading the Tree Result
stages.question: What do the reported metrics mean?
stages.miniPlan: MAE, RMSE, RSS, units, and split.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight per-row error contributions and reconcile reported numbers with current predictions.
stages.reference: MAE uses outcome units. MSE uses squared outcome units. RMSE takes the square root of MSE to return to outcome units, while emphasizing large errors. Report the sample size, split and baseline with the score. A single RMSE is not a guaranteed bound on every future error.

stages.title: Reality Check: Limitations
stages.question: What are the characteristic failure cases?
stages.miniPlan: Extrapolation, instability, staircase, and axis-aligned split thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch a labeled failure scenario; use a controlled data perturbation to show instability.
stages.reference: Axis-aligned trees test one input at a time, so diagonal patterns may need many rectangular steps. Their instability can make one fitted explanation fragile. Ensembles may reduce some variability but can still overfit, leak data or fail after a population change. Use comparable validation before choosing an alternative.

stages.title: Synthesis
stages.question: Can I reconstruct the algorithm?
stages.miniPlan: Arrange root → candidates → best split → recurse → validate → leaf.
stages.interactionPlan: Complete the sequence and explain why an ensemble may help; do not promise every ensemble removes bias.
stages.reference: Reconstruct both training and prediction. Training searches and counts only training rows. Prediction follows the saved tests without knowing the new outcome. Report cuts, growth rules, pruning, leaf averages, sample split and validation error. The rules describe predictive groups, not proven causal effects.

regression-trees.title: Regression Trees
regression-trees.intro: Predict a number by asking a sequence of yes/no questions. Follow the point through its region and tree path to one leaf average.
regression-trees.prerequisite: Averages, prediction errors, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: Points, labels, and a decision boundary
stages.question: What does a decision boundary decide?
stages.miniPlan: Signed score and class label for one point.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a point and inspect its score; reserve probability language for calibrated output.
stages.reference: A feature is an input measurement. For a linear model, score = wᵀx+b: multiply the inputs by weights and add the intercept. The boundary is score zero. A line in two inputs becomes a plane in three and a hyperplane in more. Changing score units without the fitting constraints does not create a meaningful new margin.

stages.title: Why not choose any separating line?
stages.question: Why is one separator preferable to another?
stages.miniPlan: Two correct separators with different nearest-point clearance.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide a candidate line and highlight the limiting points.
stages.reference: Training accuracy only counts which side each point lands on. A wider margin adds a geometric preference. Soft-margin fitting also allows points inside the margin and on the wrong side. A wide margin cannot repair data leakage, unreliable labels or an unrepresentative sample.

stages.title: The margin is protected space
stages.question: What is the margin?
stages.miniPlan: Decision plane versus ±1 support planes and geometric width.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the weight norm to margin width; keep functional and geometric margins distinct.
stages.reference: The score normalization places margin planes at wᵀx+b=±1. For a linear SVM, width = 2/‖w‖ in the coordinates used for fitting. Changing scaling changes that geometry. With soft margins, nearest points may lie inside or beyond these lines; the margin lines need not touch the nearest correctly classified point on each side.

stages.title: Support vectors shape the fitted separator
stages.question: Why do support vectors matter?
stages.miniPlan: A safely distant point versus a constraining point.
stages.interactionPlan: Move each in a fixed-data example and compare refits; qualify ties and soft-margin cases.
stages.reference: In the dual formulation, α_i is a fitted weight for training row i. Rows with α_i>0 are support vectors. These can constrain the separator even when they are misclassified. Support means involvement in this fitted decision, not causal or universal importance. Small movements of safely excluded points may not change a solution, but larger changes can.

stages.title: Hard margins break when reality overlaps
stages.question: Why allow violations?
stages.miniPlan: Slack 0, between 0 and 1, and above 1 examples.
stages.interactionPlan: Introduce an overlapping point and show the constrained fit; handle the boundary case ξ=1 precisely.
stages.reference: Slack ξ_i measures violation of y_i score_i≥1. ξ=0 means at or beyond the correct margin; 0<ξ<1 means inside it but on the correct side. ξ=1 reaches the decision boundary; ξ>1 is on the wrong side. Using ≤1 as always correctly classified would mishandle that boundary case. The soft-margin model penalizes slack rather than requiring every row to fit perfectly.

stages.title: C decides how expensive violations are
stages.question: What does C penalize?
stages.miniPlan: Wider margin with violations versus expensive violations.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub C on a logarithmic scale; compare actual training objective terms and validation behavior.
stages.reference: A common linear objective is ½‖w‖²+CΣ max(0,1−y_i score_i). Σ means add across training rows. Larger C gives violations more weight, so C is an inverse regularization setting. Its best value depends on the data, scale and objective. It is not a direct accuracy dial.

stages.title: Scale features before comparing distances
stages.question: Why fit scaling inside a fold?
stages.miniPlan: Training mean/SD applied to a new row.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare raw and scaled geometry with the same data; preserve feature-unit explanations.
stages.reference: Standardization is (value−training mean)/training SD. Fit those two numbers using each training fold. Apply the same values to its held-out rows. Scaling everything before splitting leaks information; fitting a separate validation scaler creates incompatible coordinates. Choose a sensible transformation for the task rather than imposing a universal scale.
stages.experiment: Change the query inputs. Subtract the saved training means, then divide by their saved SDs. Check the two transformed values before reading the receipt.

stages.title: Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
stages.question: Why do easy correct points have zero hinge loss?
stages.miniPlan: y·f(x) and max(0,1−margin).
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query along the hinge-loss curve and link its margin position.
stages.reference: Multiply the true signed label by the score. If that product is at least 1, loss is zero. At product .4, loss is .6. At product −.3, loss is 1.3. max means take the larger of zero and the calculated amount. At score zero, a separate tie rule decides the predicted class.
stages.experiment: Move the signed-margin input above and below 1. Predict when hinge loss becomes zero, then check the marked point and numeric penalty.

stages.title: The decision score is not automatically a probability
stages.question: Why is a score not a probability?
stages.miniPlan: Score / signed distance / calibrated probability distinctions.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a score and an explicitly fitted calibration example; never relabel sigmoid output as calibrated without evidence.
stages.reference: For a linear SVM, dividing score by ‖w‖ gives signed geometric distance in the fitted input scale. A kernel score is not generally literal distance in the original plotted axes. Score 2 does not mean 200% or twice the chance of score 1. Calibration maps held-out scores to estimated class probabilities under its own assumptions.

stages.title: A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern
stages.question: How can a nonlinear feature help?
stages.miniPlan: x₁, x₂, and squared radius for one point.
stages.interactionPlan: Map a ring example to radius space and show the resulting simple threshold.
stages.reference: For an inner cluster and outer ring, r²=x₁²+x₂² measures squared distance from the origin. A cutoff in r² can make a circular boundary in the original plot. Kernel similarity corresponds to inner products in a transformed feature space. The transform is a modeling choice, not extra independently observed data.

stages.title: The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion
stages.question: What does a kernel compute?
stages.miniPlan: Similarity of two selected points at two gamma values.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect an RBF influence profile; link C/gamma changes to the real fitted boundary with stale-fit cancellation.
stages.reference: RBF similarity K(x,z)=exp(−γ‖x−z‖²). exp is the exponential function. At identical inputs the value is 1; it approaches zero with increasing distance. Small gamma spreads influence more widely, while large gamma makes it local. Gamma and C interact, and an intricate training boundary may predict poorly elsewhere.

stages.title: Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation
stages.question: How do we choose C and gamma?
stages.miniPlan: Pipeline inside each inner fold, outer evaluation separate.
stages.interactionPlan: Explore a bounded validation grid; use train-fitted scaling and keep final test sealed.
stages.reference: Use a validation scheme suited to class balance, time or related groups. Compare candidates with an appropriate score, fit scaling in the pipeline, then refit the selected procedure on development data before final evaluation. A logarithmic search explores settings across orders of magnitude. A winner at a search edge calls for investigation, not a declaration of a universal optimum.

stages.title: Measure the errors the problem actually cares about
stages.question: What matters beyond accuracy?
stages.miniPlan: Error costs, minority recall, calibration, and multiclass strategy.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a concrete goal and inspect matching validation metrics; explain OVR/OVO separately from the binary illustration.
stages.reference: Precision and recall have different denominators; use both counts and rates where mistakes have different costs. One-vs-one uses K(K−1)/2 binary classifiers for K classes; one-vs-rest uses K. A well-calibrated .8 prediction corresponds to about 80% positives among comparable cases receiving that score. Raw SVM scores do not promise that frequency.

stages.title: Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back
stages.question: Can I diagnose the fitted boundary?
stages.miniPlan: Support count, chosen settings, validation result, and a query receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a labeled training point explicitly, refit, and compare; preserve a baseline and provide an equivalent form input.
stages.reference: Check solver diagnostics as well as the plot. In a bounded teaching solver, an imperfect numerical solution can differ from an ideal converged fit. Report the kernel, scaling, C, gamma, support-vector count, convergence information and useful validation errors. Large gamma can produce irregular local boundaries, but neither complexity nor its opposite proves the model suitable.

support-vector-machine.title: Support Vector Machines — Separate classes with breathing room
support-vector-machine.intro: Find a separating rule with room around its boundary. See how allowed mistakes, input scales and kernels change the fit.
support-vector-machine.prerequisite: Two-axis plots, simple distances, and training/validation splits.

stages.title: The Raw Data & The Question
stages.question: Why does row order matter?
stages.miniPlan: Two neighboring months and their dates.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare chronological and shuffled views of the same data; explain what temporal relationships shuffling breaks.
stages.reference: The date is part of the information, not just a row label. Randomly splitting rows can put later information into the training used to predict earlier times. Time order matters for this forecasting task. That does not mean every time-series study has the same splitting design; match it to the information available at deployment.

stages.title: The Time Plot
stages.question: What should I notice before modeling?
stages.miniPlan: Trend, recurring pattern, and unusual point thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Tap or focus a date to pin its value; highlight time windows without requiring a hover.
stages.reference: Trend is longer-term movement. Seasonality repeats at a known period, such as 12 months. A few similar wiggles are not enough to establish a recurring season. Check dates, missing measurements, unusual events and several cycles. These observations guide modeling but do not establish causes.

stages.title: Decomposing the Pattern
stages.question: How do components add up?
stages.miniPlan: One month's trend + seasonality + remainder.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle components on the same scale; label these as known simulation components, not estimated decomposition.
stages.reference: The additive teaching model adds its parts. Real decomposition estimates them and may have more than one reasonable answer. If seasonal swings grow with the level, a multiplicative description or transformation may be more suitable. The simulated example's known components are not fitted evidence from real demand.

stages.title: The Assumption of Stationarity
stages.question: What stays stable in a stationary process?
stages.miniPlan: Mean, variance, and lag covariance definitions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare drifting mean and changing variance separately; use a reading window without implying it proves stationarity.
stages.reference: Variance measures squared spread around the average. Autocovariance measures how two time-separated values vary together. Weak stationarity requires that relationship to depend on the lag, not the calendar date. Removing a trend does not guarantee stable variance, seasonality or dependence. A short sample plot is evidence to inspect, not proof of the full process assumptions.

stages.title: Fixing It: Differencing
stages.question: What does differencing actually subtract?
stages.miniPlan: This month − previous month, with original units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select two adjacent values and trace the resulting difference; show that differencing does not guarantee stationarity.
stages.reference: With values 10,12,15,14, first differences are 2,3,−1. Five observations give four first differences. For monthly lag-12 differencing, subtract the same month from a year earlier. Inspect the result afterward. Unnecessary differencing can add structure or noise and does not guarantee stationarity.

stages.title: Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF)
stages.question: What is a lag?
stages.miniPlan: The same series shifted by one and twelve periods.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub lag while linking paired points and the ACF bar; explain approximate bounds and multiple-lag interpretation.
stages.reference: At lag k, pair values k time steps apart. The displayed ACF adds products of their gaps from the mean and scales by the full series' squared gaps. ACF means autocorrelation function. Trend and seasonality can affect it. A large lag-12 value is a pattern to investigate, not evidence of a causal annual mechanism. This plot does not show significance bands.

stages.title: Forecasting the Future
stages.question: How do we evaluate forecasts honestly?
stages.miniPlan: Expanding-window train/validation strip.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the forecast origin forward; compare a real naive baseline, and label the current forecast fan as heuristic until calibrated intervals replace it.
stages.reference: An expanding window keeps adding earlier data; a rolling window keeps a recent segment. Compare last-value, seasonal-last-value, drift or moving-average baselines as appropriate. A fixed-origin 12-step forecast cannot use the actual value at step 11. This lab repeats the last observed 12-month season, a seasonal-naive forecast. It does not fit ARIMA or draw a forecast uncertainty interval. Future actuals are used only to score errors.

stages.title: Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals
stages.question: What patterns should residuals not retain?
stages.miniPlan: Residual definition with one date's calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle a missing seasonal component and show residual ACF; distinguish random-looking residuals from proven model validity.
stages.reference: Small random residual patterns can occur even with a suitable model. Large repeated structure suggests information the model has not captured. Forecast errors may also have horizon-dependent variance, so constant spread is not a universal requirement. Examine the model's actual error assumptions and the forecast horizon rather than demanding that every sample correlation equal zero.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.question: What belongs in a forecast report?
stages.miniPlan: Horizon, baseline, error metric, and interval meaning.
stages.interactionPlan: Link every reported number to its date range and model; avoid a nominal 95% label for an uncalibrated fan.
stages.reference: Say whether forecasts are one-step or several steps ahead. Give the starting dates, horizon, baseline and error measure. If reporting a prediction interval, state its method and assumptions about future observations. This lab draws no forecast interval. Its measured error is for a fixed-origin 12-step seasonal-naive forecast. A good short-horizon score does not establish good year-ahead forecasts.

stages.title: Limitations & Caveats
stages.question: When might yesterday stop predicting tomorrow?
stages.miniPlan: Stable period versus structural break.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a level shift and compare rolling versus expanding fitting windows; explain the conditional nature of forecasts.
stages.reference: Changes in a process are called structural breaks or drift. Historical fit cannot guarantee performance after an unprecedented change. A change in inputs is a warning, not proof that predictions fail. Inspect later outcomes, errors and data quality. Uncertainty may grow with the horizon, but the exact pattern depends on the forecasting model.

time-series-analysis.title: Time Series Analysis
time-series-analysis.intro: Put observations in time order. Learn to spot repeated patterns, describe changes, and check forecasts without using future information.
time-series-analysis.prerequisite: Averages, time plots, and prediction errors.
